relative-pronouns.intro_tr: Relative pronouns connect a subordinate clause to a noun in the main sentence (the antecedent), letting you combine two ideas into one sentence instead of repeating the noun. Unlike English, where the choice between "who/whom/which/that" often depends on whether the antecedent is a person or a thing, French relative pronouns are chosen based on the grammatical role they play inside the relative clause: subject (qui), direct object (que), object of "de" (dont), or place/time (où). The same pronoun (qui, que, dont) is used for both people and things — only the function changes which pronoun you pick. This page covers the four essential relative pronouns that handle the vast majority of everyday sentences; more advanced forms (lequel + preposition, ce qui / ce que) are covered in a separate topic.

tables.caption_tr: Overview of the Four Basic Relative Pronouns
rows: Subject of the verb in the relative clause
L'homme qui parle est mon voisin.
The man who is speaking is my neighbor.
Direct object of the verb in the relative clause
Le livre que je lis est passionnant.
The book that I am reading is fascinating.
Object introduced by the preposition 'de' (verb+de, noun+de, adjective+de)
La voiture dont je parle est rouge.
The car I'm talking about is red.
place/time expression (à, dans, en + place or time)
La ville où j'habite est belle.
The city where I live is beautiful.

tables.caption_tr: Qui vs. Que — How to Choose the Right One
rows: Yes, when the clause is in a compound tense (e.g., la pomme que j'ai mangée)
Can you say '[pronoun] + verb' with no extra subject?
Do you need to add a subject after it?

tables.caption_tr: Dont — Common Verbs, Nouns and Adjectives that Trigger It
rows: Le film dont je te parle...
The film I'm telling you about...
Le voyage dont je suis content...
Le jour dont je me souviens...
L'homme dont le fils est médecin...
The man whose son is a doctor...

tables.caption_tr: Où — Place and Time Uses
rows: city, country, room, building, region, etc.
La maison où je suis né...
The house where I was born...
Le jour où je t'ai rencontré...
La rue par où nous sommes passés...

rows: 'avoir besoin de' requires dont, not que — the verb takes 'de'.
L'homme dont la fille est médecin
Possession expressed with 'de' → dont, never que + son/sa/ses.
Le jour où je suis né

'qui' never elides before a vowel — only 'que' becomes 'qu''.

examples.target: La fille qui chante est ma sœur.
examples.translation_tr: The girl who is singing is my sister.
examples.note_tr: 'qui' = subject of 'chante'; refers to a person.

examples.target: Le film que nous avons vu était excellent.
examples.translation_tr: The movie that we saw was excellent.
examples.note_tr: 'que' = direct object of 'avons vu'; past participle 'vu' stays masculine singular to agree with 'le film'.

examples.target: Voici le collègue dont je t'ai parlé.
examples.translation_tr: Here is the colleague I told you about.
examples.note_tr: 'dont' replaces 'de ce collègue' (parler DE quelqu'un).

examples.target: C'est la maison où j'ai grandi.
examples.translation_tr: This is the house where I grew up.
examples.note_tr: 'où' refers to place, never to a person.

examples.target: Je me souviens du jour où nous nous sommes rencontrés.
examples.translation_tr: I remember the day when we met.
examples.note_tr: 'où' can also mean 'when' with time expressions (le jour, l'année, le moment).

examples.target: Les enfants dont les parents travaillent ici sont heureux.
examples.translation_tr: The children whose parents work here are happy.
examples.note_tr: 'dont' expresses possession ('leurs parents' → 'dont les parents').

examples.target: L'homme qui habite à côté est médecin.
examples.translation_tr: The man who lives next door is a doctor.
examples.note_tr: 'qui' never elides, even before a vowel: 'qui habite', not 'qu'habite'.

examples.target: La pomme que j'ai mangée était délicieuse.
examples.translation_tr: The apple that I ate was delicious.
examples.note_tr: 'que' elides to 'qu'' before a vowel; past participle 'mangée' agrees in gender/number with the feminine antecedent 'la pomme'.

plus-que-parfait.intro_tr: The plus-que-parfait ("pluperfect", literally "more than perfect") is the French tense used to express an action that happened before another past action — it is "the past of the past." It is formed with the imparfait of the auxiliary (avoir or être) plus the past participle, following exactly the same auxiliary-choice and agreement rules as the passé composé. You'll meet it constantly in narration ("when I arrived, she had already left"), in reported speech (backshifting a passé composé into the past), and in unreal past conditional sentences with si (si + plus-que-parfait → conditionnel passé). Because it always relies on the imparfait of avoir/être, mastering those two conjugations is the real key to this tense.

tables.caption_tr: Formation: imparfait of avoir/être + past participle
Imparfait of the two auxiliaries (the building block of plus-que-parfait)
Auxiliary choice and past participle agreement rules (same as passé composé)
rows: No agreement with subject; agreement with a preceding direct object (COD) only
Les lettres qu'il avait écrites (agrees with 'lettres', placed before)
Verbs of movement/state (the 'maison d'être' verbs: aller, venir, arriver, partir, entrer, sortir, monter, descendre, naître, mourir, rester, retourner, passer, tomber + their compounds)
Past participle agrees with the subject in gender and number
Agrees with the reflexive pronoun if it is the direct object; no agreement if followed by a direct object
Elle s'était lavée. / Elle s'était lavé les mains.

tables.caption_tr: Common irregular past participles used in the plus-que-parfait
When to use the plus-que-parfait: main functions
rows: Marks an action completed before another past action (in passé composé or imparfait)
Quand elle est arrivée, nous avions déjà dîné.
A passé composé in the original statement becomes plus-que-parfait when reported from a past point of view
Direct: 'J'ai perdu mes clés.' → Reported: Il a dit qu'il avait perdu ses clés.
si + plus-que-parfait, result clause in conditionnel passé
Si tu m'avais appelé, je serais venu.
Plus-que-parfait for the earlier repeated action, imparfait for the resulting habitual action
Dès qu'il avait mangé, il sortait se promener.
Regret or reproach about the past
Often combined with si seulement or je regrette que + plus-que-parfait de sentiment
Si seulement j'avais écouté mes parents !

tables.caption_tr: Timeline comparison: plus-que-parfait vs. passé composé vs. imparfait
rows: Furthest back in the past ('past of the past')
Action completed before another past action
Il avait fermé la porte avant de partir.
A completed past event, the main reference point
Single, completed past action or event
Background, ongoing state or habitual past action
Il fermait toujours la porte à clé.

examples.target: Quand je suis arrivé, il était déjà parti.
examples.translation_tr: When I arrived, he had already left.
examples.note_tr: The plus-que-parfait (était parti) shows an action completed before another past action (suis arrivé).

examples.target: Elle m'a dit qu'elle avait fini ses devoirs.
examples.translation_tr: She told me (that) she had finished her homework.
examples.note_tr: Reported speech: a passé composé in direct speech ('j'ai fini') becomes plus-que-parfait when reported in the past.

examples.target: Si j'avais su, je ne serais pas venu.
examples.translation_tr: If I had known, I wouldn't have come.
examples.note_tr: Third-type conditional sentence: si + plus-que-parfait, main clause in conditionnel passé.

examples.target: Nous avions déjà mangé quand ils sont arrivés.
examples.translation_tr: We had already eaten when they arrived.

examples.target: Il n'avait jamais vu la mer avant ce voyage.
examples.translation_tr: He had never seen the sea before this trip.
examples.note_tr: Negation wraps around the auxiliary: n'avait jamais vu.

examples.target: Dès qu'il avait terminé, il rentrait chez lui.
examples.translation_tr: As soon as he had finished, he would go home.
examples.note_tr: Habitual past sequence: plus-que-parfait for the earlier repeated action, imparfait for the following habitual result.

examples.target: Vous aviez déjà vu ce film avant hier soir.
examples.translation_tr: You had already seen this film before last night.

examples.target: Elle s'était levée avant que le soleil ne se lève.
examples.translation_tr: She had gotten up before the sun rose.
examples.note_tr: Reflexive verb: auxiliary être + reflexive pronoun s', past participle agrees with the subject (levée, feminine).

conditionnel-present.intro_tr: The Conditionnel Présent ("would" form) is built by adding the Imparfait endings (-ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient) to the same stem used for the Futur Simple (usually the infinitive). It is the go-to tense for polite requests and suggestions in French, softening statements that would otherwise sound blunt or like an order. It also expresses the result of a hypothetical situation (paired with "si + imparfait"), unconfirmed or reported information (common in news French), wishes, and imagined scenarios. Because the stem is identical to the Futur Simple, the two tenses are easy to confuse in writing — only the endings differ. Mastering this tense is essential for sounding polite and natural in everyday French, from ordering coffee to giving gentle advice.

tables.caption_tr: Formation: Conditionnel Présent Endings (stem = same as Futur Simple + Imparfait endings)
footnotes_tr: For -re verbs, drop the final 'e' from the infinitive before adding endings (vendre → vendr- → vendrais).
The endings are identical to the Imparfait endings — only the stem differs (infinitive/future stem vs. Imparfait stem).

tables.caption_tr: Irregular Conditional Stems (same irregular stems as Futur Simple)
rows: I would be able to / could
I would want / I would like
footnotes_tr: These stems are identical to the ones used for the Futur Simple; only the endings change (-ai vs -ais, etc.).

tables.caption_tr: Full Conjugation Example: vouloir (Conditionnel Présent) — the key 'politeness' verb
rows: I would like / I would want
he / she / one would like / want
you would like / want (formal or plural)
footnotes_tr: 'Je voudrais' is far more polite than 'Je veux' and is the standard way to make requests in shops, restaurants, and formal speech.

tables.caption_tr: Main Uses of the Conditionnel Présent
rows: Tu devrais..., Vous pourriez..., On pourrait...
Result of an unreal/hypothetical 'si' condition (imparfait in the si-clause)
Journalistic conditional for rumors or unverified facts
Le président serait malade (He is reportedly ill)
Describing something as if it were true
On dirait un rêve (It looks/seems like a dream)
Tu aurais pu me le dire ! (You could have told me!) — note: this needs Conditionnel Passé for past regret
footnotes_tr: The 'reported information' use is very common in news headlines and formal journalism, marking that the fact is not officially confirmed.

tables.caption_tr: Common Polite Expressions Using the Conditionnel Présent
Hypothetical Si-Clauses: Type 2 (Present Unreal Condition)
footnotes_tr: This 'si + imparfait, conditionnel présent' structure describes a present or future situation that is unreal, unlikely, or purely hypothetical — different from 'si + présent, futur' (real/likely condition) and 'si + plus-que-parfait, conditionnel passé' (unreal past condition).

tables.caption_tr: Common Confusion: Futur Simple vs. Conditionnel Présent (same stem, different ending)
footnotes_tr: In fast informal speech the two endings can sound almost identical, but in writing they must never be confused — this is one of the most common spelling mistakes among learners (and even native speakers).

examples.target: Je voudrais un café, s'il vous plaît.
examples.translation_tr: I would like a coffee, please.
examples.note_tr: Classic polite request using 'vouloir' in the conditional instead of the blunt present tense 'Je veux'.

examples.target: Pourriez-vous m'aider, s'il vous plaît ?
examples.translation_tr: Could you help me, please?
examples.note_tr: 'pouvoir' in the conditional softens a request into a polite question.

examples.target: Si j'avais plus de temps, je voyagerais davantage.
examples.translation_tr: If I had more time, I would travel more.
examples.note_tr: Hypothetical si-clause: imparfait in the 'si' part, conditionnel présent in the result.

examples.target: À ta place, je ne dirais rien.
examples.translation_tr: In your place, I wouldn't say anything.
examples.note_tr: 'À ta/votre place' + conditional is a common way to give hypothetical advice.

examples.target: Tu devrais voir un médecin.
examples.translation_tr: You should see a doctor.
examples.note_tr: 'devoir' in the conditional expresses advice, much softer than the imperative.

examples.target: Le suspect serait actuellement en fuite.
examples.translation_tr: The suspect is reportedly currently on the run.
examples.note_tr: Journalistic/'rumor' conditional: used in news reports for unverified information.

examples.target: Ça me plairait beaucoup de venir avec vous.
examples.translation_tr: I would really like to come with you.
examples.note_tr: 'plaire' in the conditional expresses a polite wish.

examples.target: On dirait qu'il va pleuvoir.
examples.translation_tr: It looks like it's going to rain.
examples.note_tr: Fixed expression 'on dirait que' = 'it looks/seems like'.

si-clauses.intro_tr: Si-clauses ('if'-sentences) join a condition to its result, and French demands a strict, fixed pairing of verb tenses across the two halves — the tense after 'si' is never the same as the tense in the main clause. There are three standard patterns, ranging from realistic conditions about the present/future, to purely hypothetical situations, to impossible conditions about the past that express regret. Each pattern has only one correct tense combination, and mixing them up (especially using a conditional tense directly after 'si') is one of the most frequent errors English speakers make. Note also that 'si' shortens to 's'' only before 'il' or 'ils', never before 'elle', 'on', 'une', etc. Finally, 'si' sometimes means 'whether' rather than 'if' — in that case none of these tense restrictions apply.

tables.caption_tr: The Three Core Types of Si-Clauses
rows: A realistic condition about present or future: if X happens, Y will/does happen
An imaginary, unlikely, or contrary-to-fact condition about now or the future: if X were true, Y would happen
A condition that did NOT happen in the past: if X had happened, Y would have happened
Mixed Type — Past Cause, Present Result
A past condition with a consequence felt in the present: if X had happened, Y would be true now

tables.caption_tr: Main-Clause Options for Type 1 (Real Condition)
rows: The result will happen later, as a consequence
Si tu étudies, tu réussiras. (If you study, you will succeed.)
A habitual truth or automatic result (general/scientific 'if')
Si on chauffe l'eau à 100°C, elle bout. (If you heat water to 100°C, it boils.)
A command, suggestion, or piece of advice
Si tu as froid, ferme la fenêtre. (If you're cold, close the window.)

tables.caption_tr: Key Irregular Verb Forms Needed for Si-Clause Patterns (je-form shown)
Common Mistakes with Si-Clauses
rows: Si j'ai le temps, je viendrai.
Never use futur simple right after conditional 'si' — use présent instead.
Never use conditionnel présent right after 'si' — use imparfait instead.
Si j'avais su, je serais venu.
Never use any conditional tense after 'si', even for past conditions — use plus-que-parfait.
'si' elides to s'' only before 'il' and 'ils'; it stays 'si' before 'elle', 'on', 'une', etc.
*Si j'aurais le temps hier, je t'aurais appelé.
Si j'avais eu le temps hier, je t'aurais appelé.
Same rule for Type 3: plus-que-parfait in the si-clause, conditionnel passé in the main clause.

tables.caption_tr: 'Si' Meaning 'If' vs 'Whether', and Similar Conjunctions
rows: Must follow the three-type tense pairing shown above
Si tu viens, on sortira. (If you come, we'll go out.)
No restriction — any tense, including futur or conditionnel, is allowed since this is not a true conditional
Je ne sais pas s'il viendra. (I don't know whether he will come.)
Même si tu pars, je resterai. (Even if you leave, I will stay.)
Je viendrai sauf s'il pleut. (I'll come unless it rains.)
Always followed by imparfait or plus-que-parfait — never présent
Il parle comme s'il savait tout. (He talks as if he knew everything.)
Followed by conditionnel (présent or passé), NOT the si-tense pattern
Prends un parapluie au cas où il pleuvrait. (Take an umbrella in case it rains.)

examples.target: Si tu as le temps, appelle-moi.
examples.translation_tr: If you have time, call me.
examples.note_tr: Type 1 (real condition): si + présent, main clause = impératif.

examples.target: Si j'ai de l'argent, j'achèterai une voiture.
examples.translation_tr: If I have money, I will buy a car.
examples.note_tr: Type 1: si + présent, main clause = futur simple.

examples.target: S'il pleut demain, nous resterons à la maison.
examples.translation_tr: If it rains tomorrow, we will stay home.
examples.note_tr: Note the elision: si + il = s'il (only before il/ils).

examples.target: Si j'étais riche, je voyagerais dans le monde entier.
examples.translation_tr: If I were rich, I would travel around the world.
examples.note_tr: Type 2 (hypothetical present): si + imparfait, main clause = conditionnel présent.

examples.target: Si tu m'avais appelé, je serais venu tout de suite.
examples.translation_tr: If you had called me, I would have come right away.
examples.note_tr: Type 3 (unreal past): si + plus-que-parfait, main clause = conditionnel passé.

examples.target: Si elle avait étudié, elle aurait réussi l'examen.
examples.translation_tr: If she had studied, she would have passed the exam.
examples.note_tr: Type 3: another example of the regret/impossible past pattern.

examples.target: Je ne sais pas s'il viendra ce soir.
examples.translation_tr: I don't know whether he will come tonight.
examples.note_tr: Here 'si' means 'whether' (indirect question), so futur is allowed after it — this is NOT a conditional si.

examples.target: Même si tu t'excusais, je ne te pardonnerais pas.
examples.translation_tr: Even if you apologized, I would not forgive you.
examples.note_tr: 'Même si' follows the same tense-pairing rules as plain 'si' (here, Type 2).

subjonctif-present.title_tr: Introduction to the Present Subjunctive (il faut que...)
subjonctif-present.intro_tr: The subjunctive (le subjonctif) is a grammatical mood used to talk about necessity, desire, emotion, doubt, or subjective judgment rather than plain fact. It almost always appears in a subordinate clause introduced by "que", after an impersonal or personal expression in the main clause. The most common trigger you will meet as a beginner is "il faut que..." ("it is necessary that..." / "one must..."), which is always followed by the subjunctive, never by the indicative. Most verbs form the present subjunctive by taking the stem of the "ils/elles" form of the present indicative and adding a fixed set of endings, but a handful of very frequent verbs (être, avoir, aller, faire, pouvoir, savoir, vouloir...) have irregular stems that must be memorized. This page focuses on recognizing the trigger "il faut que" and building correct subjunctive forms for regular and key irregular verbs.

tables.caption_tr: Formation pattern: subjunctive endings for regular verbs
footnotes_tr: The stem for je/tu/il/ils comes from the 'ils' form of the present indicative (e.g. ils parlent → parl-).
The stem for nous/vous is usually the same as the imparfait stem (often identical to the present indicative nous/vous stem).

tables.caption_tr: Full subjunctive conjugation of regular verbs (parler, finir, vendre)
footnotes_tr: Note that the endings -e, -es, -e, -ions, -iez, -ent are the same for all three groups; only the stem changes.

tables.caption_tr: Fully irregular subjunctive verbs: être and avoir
footnotes_tr: être and avoir do not follow the regular stem rule at all — their forms must simply be memorized.
These two verbs are extremely frequent after 'il faut que', so learn them first.

tables.caption_tr: Verbs with an irregular stem but regular endings (aller, faire, pouvoir, savoir, vouloir)
footnotes_tr: aller and vouloir switch to a different stem for nous/vous (all-, voul-) — this is a very common learner error.
falloir (to be necessary) only exists in the impersonal form: qu'il faille.
valoir (to be worth) follows the same pattern as aller: que je vaille, que nous valions.

tables.caption_tr: Common expressions that trigger the subjunctive after 'il faut que' and similar structures
rows: Il est nécessaire que vous veniez.
Il est important qu'il sache la vérité.
Il vaut mieux que nous soyons prudents.
Je te le dis pour que tu comprennes.
footnotes_tr: 'Il ne faut pas que' means 'must not / should not', not 'don't have to' — this negation changes the meaning, not just the mood.
All these expressions require 'que' before the subordinate clause; the subjunctive verb almost always follows immediately after 'que'.

tables.caption_tr: Indicative vs. subjunctive after similar verbs: spotting the difference
rows: Je ne pense pas qu'il vienne.
Il est sûr qu'elle a raison.
Il est possible qu'elle ait raison.
Il faut qu'elle ait raison sur ce point.
footnotes_tr: As a rule of thumb: certainty and fact → indicative; necessity, desire, emotion, doubt, or judgment → subjunctive.

examples.target: Il faut que tu fasses tes devoirs.
examples.translation_tr: You have to do your homework.
examples.note_tr: faire → que tu fasses (irregular stem fass-)

examples.target: Il faut que nous partions maintenant.
examples.translation_tr: We have to leave now.
examples.note_tr: partir is regular in the subjunctive: stem from ils partent

examples.target: Il faut que je sois à l'heure.
examples.translation_tr: I need to be on time.
examples.note_tr: être is fully irregular: que je sois

examples.target: Il faut qu'elle vienne avec nous.
examples.translation_tr: She needs to come with us.
examples.note_tr: venir → que + subjonctif is required after il faut que

examples.target: Il faut que vous ayez votre passeport.
examples.translation_tr: You must have your passport.
examples.note_tr: avoir is fully irregular: que vous ayez

examples.target: Il ne faut pas que tu dises cela.
examples.translation_tr: You must not say that.
examples.note_tr: Negating il faut changes the meaning to a prohibition, not 'don't have to'

examples.target: Il faut que nous sachions la vérité.
examples.translation_tr: We need to know the truth.
examples.note_tr: savoir → irregular stem sach-

examples.target: Il faut qu'il aille chez le médecin.
examples.translation_tr: He needs to go to the doctor.
examples.note_tr: aller → irregular stem aill- (except nous/vous, which use all-)

passive-voice.title_tr: The Passive Voice (être + Past Participle, par)
passive-voice.intro_tr: The passive voice (la voix passive) turns the object of an active sentence into the subject, shifting focus away from who performs the action to who or what receives it. It is built with être conjugated in any tense + the past participle of the main verb, and the past participle always agrees in gender and number with the new subject, exactly like an adjective. The person or thing doing the action (the "agent") is optional and, when stated, is introduced by par for concrete physical actions or by de for verbs of feeling, state, or description (aimer, respecter, entourer, couvrir...). Only verbs that take a direct object (COD) in the active voice can be turned into a passive sentence — verbs followed by à (téléphoner à, plaire à) can never be passivized. French uses the passive far less than English; the impersonal on and pronominal verbs with a passive sense (se vendre, se dire, se manger) are common, more natural alternatives.

tables.caption_tr: Active vs. Passive: How the Transformation Works
rows: La souris est mangée par le chat.
la souris (receives the action, becomes new subject)
mangée agrees with feminine singular 'la souris'

tables.caption_tr: Passive Voice Across All Major Tenses (verb: inviter → to invite)
rows: he was being invited / used to be invited
he was invited / has been invited

tables.caption_tr: Full Person Conjugation at the Présent (verb: aimer → to love)
rows: il est aimé / elle est aimée
he is loved / she is loved
ils sont aimés / elles sont aimées

tables.caption_tr: Choosing the Agent Preposition: par vs. de
rows: the verb expresses a concrete, deliberate, physical action
La lettre a été écrite par Marie. (The letter was written by Marie.)
the agent actively 'does' something to the subject
Le pont a été construit par des ingénieurs romains.
the verb expresses a feeling, opinion, or emotional state
Il est respecté de tous. (He is respected by everyone.)
the verb describes a permanent state, description, or covering/surrounding
La table est couverte de poussière. (The table is covered with dust.)
used especially with: aimer, respecter, connaître, entourer, couvrir, accompagner, suivre
Le sommet est couvert de neige.

tables.caption_tr: Common State/Feeling Verbs That Take 'de' Instead of 'par'
rows: Elle est aimée de son mari.
Il est respecté de ses employés.
Cet acteur est connu de tout le monde.
Le château est entouré d'un fossé.
Le sol était couvert de feuilles.
Le président était accompagné de ses gardes.
Il est toujours suivi de son chien.

tables.caption_tr: Past Participle Agreement Rules in the Passive
rows: Since 'être' is used, the participle behaves like an adjective and always agrees in gender and number with the grammatical subject
No ending is added for masculine singular subjects
The rule applies whether être is in présent, passé composé, futur, etc.
Elles ont été invitées. (passé composé, fem. plural)

tables.caption_tr: Restrictions: When the Passive CANNOT Be Used
rows: Verbs with no direct object cannot form a passive at all
Il est arrivé. (this is just passé composé, NOT a passive — 'arriver' has no direct object)
téléphoner à, plaire à, obéir à, nuire à cannot be passivized in standard French
Incorrect: *Elle est téléphonée. Correct (active): On lui téléphone.
These already have their own passive-like meaning and don't use être + participle + par in the same way
Ce plat se mange froid. (not: est mangé par...)
Verbs without a clear object noun
Some verbs simply don't have a natural passive equivalent in everyday usage

tables.caption_tr: Natural Alternatives to the Passive Voice
rows: on + active verb (very common when agent is people in general)
On parle français ici. (French is spoken here.)
Ce vin se boit frais. (This wine is drunk chilled.) / Ça ne se fait pas. (That isn't done.)
Active voice with a clear agent
keep the natural active structure instead of passivizing
Le facteur a livré le colis. (preferred over: Le colis a été livré par le facteur.)
used especially when the subject is a person affected by the action
Il s'est fait renvoyer. (He got fired.)

examples.target: La souris est mangée par le chat.
examples.translation_tr: The mouse is eaten by the cat.
examples.note_tr: Present tense passive; 'par' introduces the agent performing a concrete action.

examples.target: Le livre a été écrit par Victor Hugo.
examples.translation_tr: The book was written by Victor Hugo.
examples.note_tr: Passé composé passive: 'a été' + past participle, agreement with the feminine? No — 'écrit' stays masculine because subject 'le livre' is masculine singular.

examples.target: Les fenêtres seront nettoyées demain.
examples.translation_tr: The windows will be cleaned tomorrow.
examples.note_tr: Futur simple passive with no agent expressed; participle agrees with feminine plural subject 'les fenêtres'.

examples.target: Il est aimé de tous ses collègues.
examples.translation_tr: He is loved by all his colleagues.
examples.note_tr: 'de' (not 'par') is used because 'aimer' expresses a feeling/state rather than a concrete action.

examples.target: La ville était entourée de montagnes.

gerondif.intro_tr: The gérondif is a French verb form built as en + present participle (-ant), used to describe an action happening at the same time as, or in relation to, the main verb's action. It always refers back to the same subject as the main clause and functions like an adverb — it never agrees in gender or number and never changes form. The gérondif typically expresses simultaneity ("while doing"), manner or means ("by doing"), cause, or condition, all in a single compact phrase. Adding "tout" before it (tout en + -ant) reinforces the sense of simultaneity or highlights a contrast/concession. Because it is invariable and always subject-bound, mastering the gérondif mainly means learning its formation rule and recognizing when the implied subject truly matches the main clause.

tables.caption_tr: How to Form the Gérondif
rows: Conjugate the verb in the present tense, 1st person plural ('nous' form)
Remove the '-ons' ending to get the stem
Attach '-ant' to the stem to form the present participle
Place the invariable word 'en' before the participle
footnotes_tr: Only three verbs are irregular: avoir → en ayant, être → en étant, savoir → en sachant.
'En' itself never changes and is not related to the pronoun 'en'.

tables.caption_tr: Gérondif of Common Verbs (Regular & Irregular)
footnotes_tr: Spelling note: '-ger' verbs keep the 'e' (en mangeant) and '-cer' verbs keep the cedilla (en commençant) to preserve the soft sound before 'a'.
For reflexive verbs, the reflexive pronoun still agrees with the subject: en me levant, en te levant, en se levant, en nous levant, en vous levant, en se levant.

tables.caption_tr: Uses of the Gérondif
rows: Two actions happen at the same time, performed by the same subject
Il chante en conduisant. (He sings while driving.)
Explains how or by what method an action is accomplished
Elle a réussi en travaillant dur. (She succeeded by working hard.)
Gives the reason behind the main action
En insistant, il a fini par convaincre son père. (By insisting, he eventually convinced his father.)
Expresses the condition under which the main action happens
En partant maintenant, vous arriverez à l'heure. (If you leave now, you will arrive on time.)
'tout' before the gérondif stresses continuity or highlights a contradiction/concession
Tout en souriant, elle était triste. (Even while smiling, she was sad.)
footnotes_tr: The exact meaning (time, manner, cause, or condition) is usually determined by context, not by a change in form.

tables.caption_tr: Gérondif vs. Participe Présent — Key Differences
rows: Must be the same as the main clause's subject
Can refer to any noun it modifies, not necessarily the subject
Adverbial — describes how, when, or why the main action happens
Adjectival/verbal — often replaces a relative clause ('qui + verb')
Invariable (unlike a true adjective), does not agree in gender/number
Il travaille en écoutant de la musique. (He works while listening to music.)
Les enfants jouant dans le parc sont heureux. (The children playing in the park are happy.)
footnotes_tr: Both share the same -ant form of the verb; only the presence of 'en' and the reference to the subject distinguish them.

tables.caption_tr: Common Mistakes with the Gérondif
rows: Using the gérondif with a different subject than the main clause
The action of the gérondif is assumed to be done by the subject of the main verb; a mismatch creates a dangling/illogical sentence
En arrivant chez moi, j'ai appelé mes amis. (NOT: En arrivant chez moi, le téléphone a sonné.)
The gérondif has no standard compound/past form for a completed prior action
Use the past infinitive instead: après être allé, après avoir fait
These verbs need a spelling adjustment to keep the correct pronunciation before 'a'
Treating the gérondif like an English gerund used as a subject/noun
French does not use en + -ant as a noun; the infinitive is used instead
Fumer est dangereux. (NOT: En fumant est dangereux.)

indirect-speech.title_tr: Indirect Speech and Tense Agreement (le discours indirect et la concordance des temps)
indirect-speech.intro_tr: Indirect speech (le discours indirect) reports what someone said without quoting their exact words, using a subordinate clause introduced by que, si, or a question word instead of quotation marks. Three things typically change when you shift from direct to indirect speech: the VERB TENSE (if the reporting verb — dire, demander, répondre, etc. — is in a past tense, the reported verb usually shifts back one "step," a rule called la concordance des temps), the PRONOUNS and POSSESSIVES (to match the new speaker's perspective: je→il, mon→son...), and TIME/PLACE ADVERBS (aujourd'hui→ce jour-là, demain→le lendemain...). If the reporting verb is in the PRESENT tense, no tense backshift is needed — the reported clause keeps its original tense. Reported yes/no questions are introduced by si, reported wh-questions keep their question word (où, quand, comment...) but lose inversion and the question mark, and reported commands become de + infinitive.

tables.caption_tr: Tense backshift (la concordance des temps) — used ONLY when the reporting verb is in a PAST tense (il a dit que…, elle a demandé si…)
rows: « Je travaille » → il a dit qu'il travaillait
« J'ai mangé » → il a dit qu'il avait mangé
« Je dormais » → il a dit qu'il dormait
« J'avais fini » → il a dit qu'il avait fini
« Je viendrai » → il a dit qu'il viendrait
« J'aurai fini » → il a dit qu'il aurait fini
« Je voudrais » → il a dit qu'il voudrait
« J'aurais aimé » → il a dit qu'il aurait aimé
« Il faut que je parte » → il a dit qu'il fallait qu'il parte
« Pars ! » → il a dit de partir
footnotes_tr: If the reporting verb is in the PRESENT (il dit que…, elle demande si…) or FUTURE, there is NO backshift: every tense simply stays exactly as it was in the direct quote.
In careful written French the plus-que-parfait, imparfait and conditionnel are the three tenses that never change form during backshift — only présent, passé composé and futur shift.

tables.caption_tr: Reported questions: how word order and introducing words change
column_headers: How it is introduced in indirect speech
rows: « Est-ce que tu pars ? » → il a demandé si je partais

Qui, où, quand, comment, pourquoi, combien

Common reporting verbs for questions: demander, se demander, vouloir savoir, ignorer.

tables.caption_tr: Pronoun and possessive shifts when reporting someone else's words
rows: Reported speaker becomes 3rd person unless you are reporting your own earlier words
il / elle (or je, if addressed to you)
Depends on who is now speaking/listening

tables.caption_tr: Time and place adverbs: how they shift when the reporting verb is in the past
rows: « Je pars aujourd'hui » → il a dit qu'il partait ce jour-là
« Je suis arrivé hier » → il a dit qu'il était arrivé la veille
« C'était avant-hier » → il a dit que c'était l'avant-veille
« Je viendrai demain » → il a dit qu'il viendrait le lendemain
« On se voit après-demain » → il a dit qu'on se voyait le surlendemain
« Je pars ce soir » → il a dit qu'il partait ce soir-là
« Je pars la semaine prochaine » → il a dit qu'il partait la semaine suivante
« Je suis venu la semaine dernière » → il a dit qu'il était venu la semaine précédente
« Je travaille maintenant » → il a dit qu'il travaillait à ce moment-là
« Je reste ici » → il a dit qu'il restait là

If you report speech immediately (present reporting verb, same day/place), these adverbs often stay unchanged: il dit qu'il part demain.

rows: Il a dit qu'il était malade.

demander si / ce que / ce qui / (question word)

double-pronouns.intro_tr: When a French sentence needs two object pronouns at once (for example a person plus a thing, or a thing plus a place/quantity), the pronouns cannot be placed in just any order — French fixes a strict sequence before the verb. This sequence changes completely, however, in the affirmative imperative, where all pronouns move after the verb and reorganize themselves. On top of the ordering rule, pronouns like *me, te, se, le, la* elide to *m', t', s', l'* before a vowel sound, and combinations such as *m'en, t'en, s'en* or *le lui, la leur* need to be learned almost as fixed chunks because native speakers produce them instantly. This page lays out the full order, the imperative exception, the elision/contraction forms, and the most common combinations you will actually hear and use.

tables.caption_tr: Standard pronoun order — declarative sentences, negative sentences, and before an infinitive (this is the order you use MOST of the time)
rows: Slot 1 = reflexive/indirect person; Slot 2 = direct object thing/person; Slot 3 = indirect object 'to him/her/them'; Slot 4 = place/'there'; Slot 5 = 'of it/of them'

tables.caption_tr: How to read the order table: pick at most one pronoun from each slot, left to right
rows: He talks to them about it.
footnotes_tr: Note: a Slot 1 pronoun and a Slot 3 pronoun (lui/leur) never appear together in this word order — French avoids combinations like 'me lui'; a preposition + stressed pronoun is used instead, e.g. 'Il me présente à lui.'

tables.caption_tr: AFFIRMATIVE IMPERATIVE order — completely different! Pronouns move AFTER the verb and are joined with hyphens
rows: moi (m') / toi (t') / lui / nous / vous / leur
footnotes_tr: moi and toi become m' and t' before en: 'Donne-moi en' → 'Donne-m'en'.
In the NEGATIVE imperative, pronouns go back BEFORE the verb in the normal Slot 1–5 order: 'Ne me le donne pas.' (Don't give it to me.)

Nous en avons besoin. (We need it.)

negation-advanced.intro_tr: Beyond the basic ne...pas, French has a whole family of two-part negative expressions built on the same "ne + [verb] + negative word" frame: ne...jamais (never), ne...rien (nothing), ne...personne (nobody), ne...plus (no longer), ne...aucun(e) (not any), ne...ni...ni (neither...nor), and ne...que (only, a restriction, not a true negative). The tricky part for beginners is that these words don't all behave the same way: pas/jamais/plus/rien sit tightly around the conjugated verb (or the auxiliary in compound tenses), while personne, aucun, and nulle part jump to the far side of the past participle or infinitive. Several of these words can also function as the SUBJECT of the sentence (Personne ne vient, Rien ne marche), and they can be stacked together in a fixed order (ne plus jamais, ne jamais rien, etc.). Finally, negation forces most indefinite/partitive articles (un, une, des, du, de la) to shrink down to a bare "de". In spoken, informal French the "ne" is very often dropped entirely, but in writing and formal speech it must stay.

tables.caption_tr: The main advanced negative expressions
rows: We no longer live in Paris.
He has no friends at all.
Je ne vais nulle part ce week-end.
I'm not going anywhere this weekend.
Je n'aime ni le café ni le thé.
I like neither coffee nor tea.
Elle ne mange que des légumes.

tables.caption_tr: Word order: the crucial split between two families
column_headers: pas / jamais / plus / rien (tight, around verb/auxiliary)
personne / aucun / nulle part (loose, after full verb group)
rows: Je ne mange jamais de viande.
Il n'a jamais menti. / Il n'a rien dit.
Il n'a vu personne. / Il n'a trouvé aucun document.
ne pas / ne jamais / ne plus / ne rien + infinitive → Il préfère ne rien dire.
infinitive + personne/aucun/nulle part → Il préfère ne voir personne.
Je ne peux voir personne aujourd'hui.
footnotes_tr: Note the placement contrast in compound tenses: 'Il n'a rien vu' (rien BEFORE the past participle) vs 'Il n'a vu personne' (personne AFTER the past participle) — this is the single most common error zone for learners.

tables.caption_tr: Combining two negative words together (fixed order)
rows: Je n'ai plus rien à ajouter.
I have nothing more to add.
Il n'y a plus personne dans la salle.
There's no one left in the room.
Il ne veut plus jamais rien entendre à ce sujet.
He never wants to hear anything about this again.
footnotes_tr: General order rule: plus and jamais come before rien and personne when stacked (plus jamais, plus rien, jamais rien, jamais personne).

tables.caption_tr: Negative words as the SUBJECT of the sentence
rows: Ni Paul ni Marie ne sont venus.
footnotes_tr: When these words are the subject, 'ne' still appears before the verb, but there is no second negative word after it — the subject itself carries the negative meaning.

tables.caption_tr: Effect of negation on articles (de-reduction)
rows: J'ai un frère. → Je n'ai pas de frère.
Il mange des pommes. → Il ne mange pas de pommes.
Je bois du café. → Je ne bois jamais de café.
C'est une erreur. → Ce n'est pas une erreur.
footnotes_tr: This de-reduction applies after pas, jamais, plus, rien, and aucun — but NOT after 'que' (ne...que), since que is a restriction, not a real negation: 'Il ne boit que du café' keeps 'du'.

tables.caption_tr: Common mistakes and clarifications
rows: rien must go BEFORE the past participle, not after.
personne must go AFTER the past participle.
Il ne mange pas des légumes.
Il ne mange pas de légumes.
des must reduce to de under negation.
Elle ne mange pas que des légumes. (meaning 'only')
Elle ne mange que des légumes.
ne...que never takes 'pas' — 'pas' + 'que' together would mean 'not only', a different meaning.
personne already carries the negative; don't add 'pas' as well.
Never combine 'pas' with another negative word (jamais, rien, personne, plus) — French negation is not double in this sense.

verbs-with-prepositions.title_tr: Verbs with Prepositions: penser à, parler de, réussir à
verbs-with-prepositions.intro_tr: Many French verbs must be followed by a specific preposition (à or de) before a noun or an infinitive, and often that preposition does not match what English speakers expect — English "to think about" becomes "penser à", "to talk about" becomes "parler de", and "to succeed in" becomes "réussir à". There is no shortcut: each verb's preposition (or lack of one) simply has to be memorized as part of the verb itself. This matters even more when the following word is replaced by a pronoun, because "à + thing" becomes the pronoun y, "de + thing" becomes the pronoun en, but "à/de + person" usually stays as à/de + a stressed pronoun (lui, elle, eux...). Below you'll find verbs grouped by their preposition, verbs with zero preposition before an infinitive, and the pronoun-replacement rules that trip up beginners the most.

to succeed in, to pass (an exam)

tables.caption_tr: Verbs followed by de + noun/pronoun (person or thing)
rows: Ne te moque pas de lui.

rows: réussir à, apprendre à, commencer à, hésiter à, s'habituer à, arriver à, se mettre à, tenir à

empêcher qqn de, remercier qqn de, féliciter qqn de, convaincre qqn de
vouloir, pouvoir, devoir, savoir, aimer, adorer, détester, préférer, espérer, falloir, aller, venir + infinitive

tables.caption_tr: Replacing à/de + noun with pronouns y and en

Vous parlez de ce livre ? — Oui, on en parle. / Vous parlez de Paul ? — Oui, on parle de lui.

interrogative-pronouns.intro_tr: French has two families of interrogative pronouns that beginners often confuse: the "simple" set (qui, que, quoi, and their long compound forms like qu'est-ce qui) used to ask "who?" or "what?", and the "selective" set (lequel, laquelle, lesquels, lesquelles) used to ask "which one(s)?" out of a known group. The choice between qui, que, and quoi depends on two things at once: whether you're asking about a person or a thing, and what grammatical role the answer will play (subject, direct object, or object of a preposition). Each simple pronoun also has a short form (which usually forces inversion of subject and verb) and a longer, more conversational "est-ce que/qui" form that keeps normal word order. Lequel is different: it doesn't distinguish person vs. thing, only agrees in gender and number with the noun it replaces, and — like the definite article — contracts with the prepositions à and de. Mastering this topic means memorizing two grids (the qui/que/quoi grid and the lequel + à/de grid) rather than a single rule.

tables.caption_tr: Table 1 — The Core Grid: Person vs. Thing, by Grammatical Function
rows: — (no short form exists; use the long form)
Object of a preposition (à, de, avec, pour...)
Standing alone / at the end of a sentence
footnotes_tr: Short subject/object forms of qui trigger subject-verb inversion or require 'est-ce que' unless the question word IS the subject (e.g. 'Qui vient ?' needs no inversion because qui is already the subject).
There is no short subject form for things — you cannot say 'Que se passe-t-il' to mean 'what is happening'; you must say 'Qu'est-ce qui se passe'.
'Quoi' by itself (Quoi ?) is common in spoken French but considered blunt/informal; 'Pardon ?' or 'Comment ?' is more polite.

tables.caption_tr: Table 2 — Short Form vs. Long Form: Word Order Differences
rows: Requires inversion of subject and verb (verb-subject), except when qui is already the subject
Long form (qui est-ce qui / que, qu'est-ce qui / que)
Keeps normal subject-verb order — no inversion needed
Qu'est-ce que tu fais ? / Qui est-ce que tu vois ?
Qui as subject (no inversion either way)

tout-usage.title_tr: Uses of tout (tout, toute, tous, toutes)
tout-usage.intro_tr: The word tout is one of the most flexible words in French: depending on context it can be an adjective, a pronoun, an adverb, or even a noun. Its spelling changes according to gender and number — tout, toute, tous, toutes — but the rule for choosing the right form is different for each grammatical role. As an adjective, tout agrees with the noun it describes and can mean 'every', 'all', or 'the whole'. As a pronoun, it stays tout when referring to an abstract 'everything', but becomes tous/toutes when referring to a group of people or things already mentioned. As an adverb (meaning 'completely' or 'quite'), it is normally invariable, except before a feminine adjective that begins with a consonant or an aspirate h, where it becomes toute/toutes to ease pronunciation. This page organizes every function of tout into clear reference tables, including its many fixed expressions.

connectors-basic.title_tr: Connectors: parce que, donc, pourtant, alors que
connectors-basic.intro_tr: French connectors link ideas of cause, consequence, and contrast, and each of the four words here has its own grammatical behavior. "Parce que" answers the question "pourquoi?" and introduces a dependent clause explaining a reason. "Donc" signals the result of what was just said and joins two independent clauses. "Pourtant" marks a surprising contrast between two facts, while "alors que" introduces a dependent clause that either contrasts two situations or shows two actions happening at the same time. Getting these right matters because French distinguishes carefully between connectors that can start a sentence, connectors that require a comma, and connectors that are followed by a full independent clause versus a subordinate one.

tables.caption_tr: Overview of the Four Core Connectors
rows: expresses contrast between two situations, or simultaneous actions
footnotes_tr: Subordinating connectors can begin the sentence (with the main clause following); coordinating connectors sit between two clauses that could each stand alone.

depuis-pendant-il-y-a.title_tr: Time Expressions: depuis, pendant, il y a, dans
depuis-pendant-il-y-a.intro_tr: Depuis, pendant, il y a, and dans are four short words that all translate loosely to English time expressions, but they are NOT interchangeable — each one forces a specific tense and points the sentence in a specific time direction. Depuis links an action that started in the past to the present moment ("since/for"), and famously requires the PRESENT tense in French where English uses a perfect tense ("I have lived here since..."). Pendant describes a bounded, complete duration and works with any tense. Il y a means "ago" and looks backward from now, while dans means "in" and looks forward from now — they are mirror opposites. Getting the tense wrong is the single most common English-speaker mistake with these words, so pay close attention to the "Tense Used" columns below.

subjonctif-usage.title_tr: Uses of the Subjunctive (wish, emotion, doubt)
subjonctif-usage.intro_tr: The subjunctive mood (subjonctif) is used in subordinate clauses introduced by "que" whenever the main clause expresses something subjective rather than an objective fact: a wish, an emotion, a doubt, a necessity, a judgment, or a purpose. Unlike the indicative, which states what is real or certain, the subjunctive signals that the speaker is talking about something wanted, feared, doubted, or merely possible. Most triggers require a change of subject between the two clauses (Je veux qu'il parte); when the subject stays the same, French normally switches to an infinitive instead (Je veux partir). Certain conjunctions (bien que, pour que, avant que...) always impose the subjunctive regardless of subject. This page assumes you already know how to conjugate the subjunctive present (see the companion page on subjunctive present formation) and focuses purely on when to use it.

subjonctif-passe.intro_tr: The subjonctif passé (past subjunctive) is a compound tense used to express that an action happened BEFORE the action of the main clause, while the whole sentence still requires the subjunctive mood (opinion, emotion, doubt, wish, certain conjunctions, superlatives, etc.). It is built exactly like the passé composé, but the auxiliary verb (avoir or être) is put into the subjonctif présent instead of the indicative present. All the usual passé composé rules still apply: same choice of auxiliary, same past participle agreement with être-verbs and with preceding direct objects, and the same irregular participles. In practice, it lets you say things like "I'm glad you finished" (aies fini) instead of just "I'm glad you finish" (finisses).

examples.target: Il faut que tu te sois reposé avant le voyage.
examples.translation_tr: You must have rested before the trip. (lit. It's necessary that you have rested...)

examples.target: Elle est surprise que nous ayons oublié son anniversaire.
examples.translation_tr: She's surprised that we forgot her birthday.

conditionnel-passe.title_tr: Conditionnel Passé & the Unreal Past (si + plus-que-parfait)
conditionnel-passe.intro_tr: The conditionnel passé (past conditional) is used to talk about actions that would have happened under different past circumstances — but didn't. It is built with the conditionnel présent of avoir or être plus a past participle, exactly like other compound tenses. Its most common job is to form the "unreal past" (often called the third conditional): Si + plus-que-parfait, ... conditionnel passé, describing a hypothetical past condition and its imagined (but unfulfilled) result. It is also used on its own — without any si-clause — to express regret, reproach, or unconfirmed information (very common in journalism). Since it relies on two tenses you must already know well (plus-que-parfait and conditionnel présent), review those first if they feel shaky.

tables.caption_tr: Step 1 — The auxiliary: conditionnel présent of avoir and être
footnotes_tr: The conditionnel passé is simply this auxiliary (in conditionnel présent) + a past participle — the same pattern as passé composé, but with a different auxiliary tense.

tables.caption_tr: Step 2 — Full conjugation with a past participle (three verb types)
footnotes_tr: With être-verbs (and reflexive verbs), the past participle agrees in gender/number with the subject, just like in passé composé.
With avoir-verbs, the past participle only agrees with a preceding direct object: 'La lettre qu'il aurait écrite...' (the letter he would have written).

tables.caption_tr: The three conditional sentence types compared
rows: If you come (and you might), we'll eat.
Si j'avais de l'argent, je voyagerais.
If I had money (but I don't), I would travel.
Si j'avais eu de l'argent, j'aurais voyagé.
If I had had money (but I didn't, in the past), I would have traveled.
footnotes_tr: This page focuses on the 3rd type: a past condition that was NOT met, and a past result that therefore never happened.
Never use 'si' + conditionnel in French — 'si' is always followed by présent, imparfait, or plus-que-parfait, never by a conditionnel form.

tables.caption_tr: Si + plus-que-parfait, ... conditionnel passé — clause order is flexible
rows: Si nous avions su, nous serions restés. (If we had known, we would have stayed.)
Nous serions restés si nous avions su. (We would have stayed if we had known.)
Si tu n'avais pas menti, je t'aurais cru. (If you hadn't lied, I would have believed you.)
Si elle m'avait écouté, elle ne serait pas tombée. (If she had listened to me, she wouldn't have fallen.)

tables.caption_tr: Frequently needed irregular past participles
rows: j'aurais pu (I would have been able to)
je serais venu(e) (I would have come)

tables.caption_tr: Uses of conditionnel passé beyond 'si' sentences
rows: Vous auriez dû réserver à l'avance. (You should have booked in advance.)
Il aurait pu m'appeler. (He could have called me.)
J'aurais aimé être là. (I would have liked to be there.)
reports an unverified past fact, softer than passé composé
Le suspect aurait quitté le pays. (The suspect reportedly left the country.)
Hypothetical result without stating the condition
À ta place, je n'aurais jamais accepté. (In your place, I would never have accepted.)

tables.caption_tr: Common mistakes and how to fix them
rows: Si j'aurais su, je serais venu.
'si' is never followed by a conditionnel form
Si j'avais su, je serais venu.
confuses futur antérieur (aurai) with conditionnel passé (aurais)
forgot past-participle agreement with être-verb subject
Si j'avais du temps, j'aurais voyagé.
mixes 2nd type si-clause (imparfait) with 3rd type main clause — tenses must match within one type
Si j'avais eu du temps, j'aurais voyagé. (both 3rd type) OR Si j'avais du temps, je voyagerais. (both 2nd type)

examples.target: Si j'avais su, je serais venu plus tôt.
examples.translation_tr: If I had known, I would have come earlier.

examples.target: Elle aurait réussi si elle avait travaillé plus.
examples.translation_tr: She would have succeeded if she had worked harder.

examples.target: Nous serions arrivés à l'heure si nous n'avions pas raté le train.
examples.translation_tr: We would have arrived on time if we hadn't missed the train.

examples.target: Tu aurais dû me le dire.
examples.translation_tr: You should have told me. (regret/reproach, no 'si' clause needed)

examples.target: Selon la presse, le président aurait démissionné hier.
examples.translation_tr: According to the press, the president reportedly resigned yesterday. (unconfirmed information)

examples.target: J'aurais aimé vous aider, mais je n'étais pas là.
examples.translation_tr: I would have liked to help you, but I wasn't there.

examples.target: Si tu m'avais appelé, je t'aurais expliqué la situation.
examples.translation_tr: If you had called me, I would have explained the situation to you.

examples.target: Ils se seraient perdus sans le GPS.
examples.translation_tr: They would have gotten lost without the GPS.

futur-anterieur.intro_tr: The futur antérieur ("future perfect") expresses an action that WILL HAVE been completed before another future action or moment. It is formed with the futur simple of avoir or être plus the past participle, following the exact same auxiliary-choice and agreement rules as the passé composé. Its two main jobs are: (1) marking anteriority inside a future time frame, almost always triggered by time connectors like quand, dès que, une fois que, aussitôt que, and après que when the main clause is in the futur simple; and (2) expressing a supposition or guess about something that has probably already happened (epistemic use, similar to English "must have"). A key trap for English speakers: after quand/dès que/etc., French requires futur antérieur (or futur simple) where English uses a present or present-perfect form — never "will" in the subordinate clause.

tables.caption_tr: Formation: futur simple of avoir/être (the auxiliary) + past participle
footnotes_tr: Choose avoir or être exactly as you would for the passé composé (most verbs take avoir; a fixed list of ~17 verbs of movement/state plus all reflexive verbs take être).

tables.caption_tr: Full conjugation example: parler (avoir-group) vs. partir (être-group)
footnotes_tr: With être, the past participle agrees in gender and number with the subject, exactly like in the passé composé.

tables.caption_tr: Reflexive verb example: se lever (futur antérieur)
rows: il se sera levé / elle se sera levée
ils se seront levés / elles se seront levées
footnotes_tr: All reflexive (pronominal) verbs use être as the auxiliary; the reflexive pronoun goes right before the auxiliary.

tables.caption_tr: When to use the futur antérieur
rows: One future action finishes before another future action/moment; almost always with a time connector.
Dès que j'aurai mangé, je partirai.
Marks completion by a specific future point in time.
Expresses a guess/probability about something that has likely already happened; often stands alone, no future meaning at all.
Il n'a pas répondu ; il aura oublié son téléphone.
Occasionally used to comment on something already accomplished, viewed from a future vantage point.
Nous aurons tout essayé, au moins.

tables.caption_tr: Time connectors that trigger futur antérieur (in the earlier-action clause) when the main clause is futur simple
rows: Quand elle aura fini, elle nous rejoindra.
Dès que vous aurez signé, envoyez le document.
Aussitôt qu'ils seront arrivés, on commencera.
Une fois que j'aurai payé, je récupérerai la clé.
Après qu'il aura parlé, nous poserons des questions.
footnotes_tr: ENGLISH TRAP: English uses a present or present-perfect tense after these connectors ('when I finish', 'as soon as she has arrived'), never 'will'. French REQUIRES a future tense (futur simple or futur antérieur) in both clauses when the overall meaning is future.

tables.caption_tr: Futur Antérieur vs. Futur Simple vs. Passé Composé — quick contrast
rows: A future action completed BEFORE another future action/moment
J'aurai fini le travail avant ton arrivée.
I will have finished the work before you arrive.
A completed past action (from the speaker's present viewpoint)

tables.caption_tr: Common irregular past participles (needed to build the futur antérieur)
footnotes_tr: The past participle form and agreement rules are identical to those used in the passé composé.

examples.target: Quand j'aurai fini mes devoirs, je sortirai avec mes amis.
examples.translation_tr: When I have finished (will have finished) my homework, I will go out with my friends.
examples.note_tr: French uses futur antérieur after 'quand' when the main clause is future; English typically uses the present perfect here, not 'will have.'

examples.target: Dès que tu seras arrivé(e), appelle-moi.
examples.translation_tr: As soon as you arrive (have arrived), call me.
examples.note_tr: 'être' verb — past participle agrees with the subject: arrivé/arrivée/arrivés/arrivées.

examples.target: Il aura terminé le rapport avant midi.
examples.translation_tr: He will have finished the report before noon.
examples.note_tr: Straightforward future-perfect meaning, same as English.

examples.target: Elle n'est pas venue ; elle aura eu un empêchement.
examples.translation_tr: She didn't come; she must have had something come up.
examples.note_tr: Epistemic use: futur antérieur expresses a guess/supposition about a past event, not a real future.

examples.target: Une fois que nous aurons mangé, nous irons au cinéma.
examples.translation_tr: Once we have eaten, we will go to the movies.
examples.note_tr: 'une fois que' behaves like 'quand'/'dès que' and requires futur antérieur for the prior action.

examples.target: Vous aurez fini ce travail d'ici vendredi.
examples.translation_tr: You will have finished this work by Friday.
examples.note_tr: Used with a deadline expression ('d'ici' + time).

examples.target: Aussitôt qu'ils seront rentrés, ils nous téléphoneront.
examples.translation_tr: As soon as they get home (have gotten home), they will call us.
examples.note_tr: 'rentrer' takes être; agreement with the plural subject 'ils' gives 'rentrés.'

examples.target: À cette heure-ci demain, j'aurai passé mon examen.
examples.translation_tr: By this time tomorrow, I will have taken my exam.
examples.note_tr: Classic future-perfect 'by [future time]' construction.

past-infinitive.intro_tr: The past infinitive (infinitif passé) expresses an action completed before another action, when both actions share the same subject. It is most commonly introduced by the conjunction 'après' ('after'), forming the pattern 'après avoir/être + past participle'. It is built with the infinitive of avoir or être plus the past participle of the main verb, following the exact same auxiliary-choice rules as the passé composé. When être is the auxiliary — including with all reflexive verbs — the past participle must agree in gender and number with the subject. This compact structure is a stylish alternative to a full subordinate clause with 'après que' or 'quand', and is frequently tested at B2 level.

tables.caption_tr: Formation of the Past Infinitive
footnotes_tr: The être group includes the classic 'DR & MRS VANDERTRAMP' verbs (devenir, revenir, monter, rester, sortir, venir, aller, naître, descendre, entrer, rentrer, tomber, retourner, arriver, mourir, partir) plus their compounds.
For reflexive verbs, the reflexive pronoun (m', t', s', nous, vous, s') always comes directly before 'être', matching the subject.

tables.caption_tr: Agreement Patterns with être in the Past Infinitive
footnotes_tr: With avoir as the auxiliary, the past participle normally stays invariable unless a preceding direct object triggers agreement (see advanced participle agreement).

tables.caption_tr: Negative Past Infinitive
footnotes_tr: Unlike simple infinitive negation, both 'ne' and 'pas' stay together directly before the auxiliary infinitive: 'ne pas avoir fait', never 'avoir ne pas fait'.

tables.caption_tr: Past Infinitive vs. Related Structures
rows: Après avoir mangé, il est sorti.
Requires the same subject for both actions; shows the first action is completed before the second.
Après qu'il a mangé, il est sorti.
Used when the two actions have different subjects, or in more explicit/formal style.
Avant de manger, il s'est lavé les mains.
Expresses the action that happens before, viewed from the opposite direction.
En mangeant, il regardait la télé.
Expresses two simultaneous actions, not a sequence.
More literary equivalent of 'après avoir mangé', dropping 'après'.

tables.caption_tr: Common Verbs — Quick Reference for the Past Infinitive

examples.target: Après avoir mangé, il est parti.
examples.translation_tr: After eating (having eaten), he left.

examples.target: Après être arrivée à Paris, Marie a appelé ses parents.
examples.translation_tr: After arriving in Paris, Marie called her parents.
examples.note_tr: 'arrivée' agrees with the feminine subject Marie because the auxiliary is être.

examples.target: Après nous être levés tôt, nous avons pris le petit-déjeuner.
examples.translation_tr: After getting up early, we had breakfast.
examples.note_tr: Reflexive past infinitive: 's'être' becomes 'nous être', and the participle agrees with the subject (masculine plural here).

examples.target: Après avoir fini ses devoirs, il a regardé la télévision.
examples.translation_tr: After finishing his homework, he watched television.

examples.target: Merci de m'avoir aidé pendant ce projet.
examples.translation_tr: Thank you for having helped me during this project.

examples.target: Après ne pas avoir dormi de la nuit, elle était épuisée.
examples.translation_tr: Having not slept all night, she was exhausted.
examples.note_tr: Both negation words 'ne' and 'pas' stay together right before the auxiliary infinitive.

examples.target: Après être sortis, ils ont fermé la porte à clé.
examples.translation_tr: After going out, they locked the door.

examples.target: Excusez-moi d'être arrivé en retard à la réunion.
examples.translation_tr: Excuse me for arriving late to the meeting.

participle-clauses.title_tr: Participle Clauses (ayant terminé, une fois parti)
participle-clauses.intro_tr: Participle clauses let you pack a subordinate idea (time, cause, or condition) into a compact phrase built around a participle, without using a conjunction like quand or parce que. French uses three participle shapes for this job: the simple present participle (parlant), the simple past participle used on its own (une fois parti), and the perfect/compound participle (ayant terminé, étant parti) for an action completed before the main clause. The participle can share the subject of the main clause, or it can bring its own subject in an "absolute" construction (le travail terminé, nous sommes partis). This structure is mostly a feature of formal writing and narration, and the trickiest point is choosing ayant vs étant and getting the agreement right.

tables.caption_tr: The three participle forms
footnotes_tr: The 'nous' stem rule: take the nous-form of the present tense, drop -ons, add -ant (nous parlons → parlant; nous finissons → finissant).

tables.caption_tr: Irregular present participles
footnotes_tr: Note the adjectival cousins of some present participles are spelled differently: savoir → sachant (verb) but 'savant' (adjective, learned); différer → différant (verb) but 'différent' (adjective).

tables.caption_tr: Types of participial clauses and their meaning
rows: Voyant qu'il pleuvait, elle prit un parapluie.
Seeing that it was raining, she took an umbrella.
action completed just before the main clause (cause or sequence)
Ayant terminé son travail, il rentra chez lui.
Having finished his work, he went home.
une fois / sitôt / à peine + past participle, main clause
Une fois arrivé, il téléphona à sa mère.
Once he arrived, he called his mother.
Absolute clause with its own subject
noun/pronoun + past or present participle, main clause (no conjunction)
cause or time, subject differs from the main clause
Le travail terminé, nous sommes partis.
The work being finished, we left.
Dinner being over, they went out.

tables.caption_tr: Agreement rules
rows: Les enfants, courant dans le jardin, riaient.
agrees in gender/number like a normal adjective
une eau courante / des enfants obéissants
Past participle in an absolute clause
agrees with the noun it refers to, like an adjective
La porte fermée, il partit. / Les devoirs finis, ils sortirent.
follows normal avoir-agreement rules: no agreement unless a preceding direct object controls it
Ayant fini ses devoirs, elle sortit. / Les leçons qu'il avait apprises, ...
past participle agrees with the subject, like all être-verbs
Étant arrivée en retard, elle s'excusa. (subject = elle, feminine)
footnotes_tr: Choosing ayant vs étant follows the same rule as choosing avoir vs être in the passé composé: être-verbs (aller, arriver, partir, the 'house of être' verbs, and all reflexive verbs) take étant; everything else takes ayant.

tables.caption_tr: Common words introducing a participial clause
rows: Une fois le repas terminé, ils ont débarrassé la table.
À peine sorti, il a commencé à pleuvoir.
Aussitôt arrivé, il a appelé sa femme.
footnotes_tr: 'À peine' at the start of a clause usually triggers subject-verb inversion in the following main clause in formal style: À peine était-il sorti qu'il commença à pleuvoir.

tables.caption_tr: Participle clauses vs. similar-looking structures
column_headers: Same subject as main clause required?
rows: En sortant, il a fermé la porte. (= as/while he went out)
No — can have its own subject (absolute)
Le temps le permettant, nous sortirons. (weather ≠ subject of 'sortirons')
Après avoir mangé, il est parti.
footnotes_tr: Do not confuse the gérondif (always 'en + -ant', same subject) with the bare present participle clause (no 'en', can take its own subject). This is a classic B2 confusion point.

examples.target: Ayant terminé ses devoirs, elle est sortie jouer.
examples.translation_tr: Having finished her homework, she went out to play.
examples.note_tr: Perfect participle (ayant + past participle) shows the action completed before the main clause.

examples.target: Une fois le contrat signé, les travaux ont commencé.
examples.translation_tr: Once the contract was signed, the work began.
examples.note_tr: 'Une fois' + past participle = absolute clause; 'signé' agrees with 'le contrat' (masculine).

examples.target: Étant arrivés en retard, ils se sont excusés auprès du professeur.
examples.translation_tr: Having arrived late, they apologized to the teacher.
examples.note_tr: 'Étant' is used because 'arriver' takes être in the compound past; the participle agrees with the plural subject 'ils'.

examples.target: Le soleil couché, la température a rapidement chuté.
examples.translation_tr: Once the sun had set, the temperature quickly dropped.
examples.note_tr: Absolute construction with its own subject 'le soleil'; no conjunction, no auxiliary — 'étant' is understood.

examples.target: Sitôt le repas fini, les enfants ont couru jouer dehors.
examples.translation_tr: As soon as the meal was finished, the children ran to play outside.
examples.note_tr: 'Sitôt' + past participle expresses immediacy, similar to 'une fois'.

examples.target: Ayant beaucoup voyagé, elle parle plusieurs langues.
examples.translation_tr: Having traveled a lot, she speaks several languages.
examples.note_tr: Cause/reason reading of the perfect participle clause.

examples.target: La réunion terminée, chacun est rentré chez soi.
examples.translation_tr: The meeting being over, everyone went home.
examples.note_tr: Absolute participial clause; 'terminée' agrees with feminine 'réunion'.

examples.target: N'ayant pas reçu de réponse, il a rappelé le lendemain.
examples.translation_tr: Not having received a reply, he called back the next day.
examples.note_tr: Negation wraps around the auxiliary: ne + ayant + pas.

causative-faire.title_tr: The Causative Construction with faire (faire faire, se faire + infinitive)
causative-faire.intro_tr: The causative construction "faire + infinitive" lets a subject cause, arrange for, or force someone else to perform an action, rather than doing it themselves (e.g. "faire réparer" = to have [something] repaired). Word order changes depending on how many participants the sentence has: just an infinitive and a "causee" (the person made to act), just an infinitive and an object, or both an object and a causee together (introduced by à or par). The reflexive variant "se faire + infinitive" shifts the focus onto the subject: it can mean arranging something for oneself ("se faire couper les cheveux" = to get one's hair cut) or, very commonly, experiencing something happen to oneself, often unwillingly, functioning almost like a passive ("se faire voler" = to get robbed). A key grammar trap: the past participle "fait" in this construction is always invariable — it never agrees with a preceding direct object, unlike ordinary avoir-verbs. Object pronouns generally attach directly before the conjugated form of "faire", and when both an object and a causee are pronominalized, the causee becomes an indirect object pronoun (lui/leur).

tables.caption_tr: Word Order Patterns in faire + infinitive (faire faire)
rows: I have the doctor come / I send for the doctor.
Je fais réparer la voiture par un mécanicien. / Il fait lire le livre à son fils.
I'm having the car repaired by a mechanic. / He has his son read the book.
(causee →) COI pronoun + COD pronoun + faire + infinitive
footnotes_tr: When both an object and a causee are present, the causee is usually introduced by à; par is used mainly when it could be confused with the direct object, or for emphasis on the agent (e.g. with a verb that already takes à for its own object).

tables.caption_tr: Conjugating faire in the Causative Frame (example: faire construire une maison — to have a house built)
footnotes_tr: Only "faire" is conjugated for tense and person; the second verb always stays in the infinitive.
In compound tenses, "fait" never agrees with a preceding direct object pronoun — it is fixed and invariable.

tables.caption_tr: Object Pronoun Placement with faire faire
rows: Je le fais venir. (I have him come.)
Je la fais réparer. (I'm having it repaired — la = the car.)
COD pronoun + COI pronoun + faire + infinitive
Je la lui fais réparer. (I have him/her repair it.)
footnotes_tr: In negative and non-imperative sentences, pronouns attach before the conjugated "faire", not before the infinitive.

tables.caption_tr: Meanings and Uses of se faire + infinitive
rows: Elle se fait couper les cheveux.
Passive / experiential — something happens to the subject, often unwillingly
Il s'est fait voler son portefeuille.
He got his wallet stolen (it happened to him).
Undergoing an action performed by a named agent
Elle s'est fait gronder par le prof.
She got scolded by the teacher.
se faire avoir / se faire plaisir / se faire des amis
to get conned / to treat oneself / to make friends.
footnotes_tr: se faire + infinitive is far more common in spoken French than the true passive (être + past participle) for describing something happening to someone.

tables.caption_tr: Past Participle Agreement: The Invariable "fait" Rule
rows: Unlike ordinary avoir-verbs, "fait" never agrees with a preceding direct object, even a feminine or plural one
Je les ai fait venir. (NOT "faites", even though "les" is feminine plural.)
Same invariability applies to se faire
The reflexive form also keeps "fait" unchanged, regardless of the subject's gender/number
Elle s'est fait couper les cheveux. (NOT "faite")
Contrast: laisser (to let) CAN agree in some cases
This is a classic point of confusion — laisser + infinitive follows different, looser agreement rules than faire
Je les ai laissé(s) partir. (agreement optional/debated) vs. Je les ai fait partir. (never agrees)
footnotes_tr: Treat "fait" as frozen/invariable whenever it directly precedes an infinitive in this construction — this is one of the most frequently tested points in French grammar exams.

tables.caption_tr: faire faire vs. se faire vs. rendre — Avoiding Common Confusions
rows: Subject causes/arranges for someone else to do the action
Je fais laver la voiture. (I have the car washed.)
Subject has something done to/for themselves, or something happens to them
Je me fais laver les cheveux. (I get my hair washed.)
Subject causes someone/something to become a certain state (NOT an action — uses an adjective, not an infinitive)
Ça me rend heureux. (That makes me happy.) — NOT "ça me fait heureux".
Subject permits/allows an action, without necessarily arranging or causing it
Je laisse mon fils regarder la télé. (I let my son watch TV.)
footnotes_tr: A very common English-speaker error is using "faire" with an adjective to mean 'make someone [adjective]' — French requires "rendre" for that meaning, reserving "faire" for causing an action (infinitive).

examples.target: Je fais réparer ma voiture.
examples.translation_tr: I'm having my car repaired.
examples.note_tr: Object only ("ma voiture") — the mechanic (causee) is left unspecified.

examples.target: Elle fait pleurer son petit frère.
examples.translation_tr: She makes her little brother cry.
examples.note_tr: "pleurer" is intransitive, so "son petit frère" is the direct object of faire.

examples.target: Nous avons fait construire une maison.
examples.translation_tr: We had a house built.
examples.note_tr: "fait" stays invariable — it never agrees with "maison".

examples.target: Il fait faire ses devoirs à son fils.
examples.translation_tr: He makes his son do his homework.
examples.note_tr: Object ("ses devoirs") + causee introduced by à ("à son fils").

examples.target: Je le lui fais lire.
examples.translation_tr: I have him read it.
examples.note_tr: "le" = the book (COD), "lui" = the causee (COI); both pronouns precede "fais".

examples.target: Je me fais couper les cheveux tous les mois.
examples.translation_tr: I get my hair cut every month.
examples.note_tr: Reflexive causative — the subject arranges for the action to be done to/for themselves.

examples.target: Elle s'est fait voler son sac.
examples.translation_tr: She had her bag stolen. / Her bag got stolen on her.
examples.note_tr: Passive/experiential use of se faire — something happens to the subject, usually unwanted.

examples.target: Ils se sont fait avoir.
examples.translation_tr: They got conned / taken for a ride.
examples.note_tr: Fixed idiomatic expression with se faire; "fait" and "avoir" never change form here.

agreement-advanced.title_tr: Advanced Past Participle Agreement (fronted direct object, reflexive verbs)
agreement-advanced.intro_tr:
This topic covers the two trickiest agreement rules for the past participle in compound tenses: (1) with avoir, the participle agrees with a direct object (COD) only when that object is placed BEFORE the verb (as a pronoun, via a relative clause with 'que', or after 'combien de' / 'quel'); a COD that follows the verb, or the pronoun 'en', never triggers agreement. (2) With reflexive (pronominal) verbs, the auxiliary is always être, but agreement does NOT simply follow être — you must check whether the reflexive pronoun itself functions as the direct object; if the verb already has its own direct object (often a body part) or is inherently indirect (like se parler, se nuire), the participle stays invariable. Mastering this requires identifying, for every sentence, exactly which word is the true direct object and where it sits relative to the verb. These rules are largely a feature of written/formal French — in spoken French the difference is often inaudible (e.g. mangé/mangée sound the same), but it matters greatly in writing, exams, and formal registers.</intro_tr>
<parameter name="related_slugs">null

tables.caption_tr: Rule 1 — Agreement with AVOIR: does the direct object (COD) come before or after?
rows: COD comes AFTER the verb (normal word order)
No agreement — participle stays in its base masculine singular form
J'ai mangé des pommes. (no agreement, COD 'des pommes' follows)
Participle AGREES in gender and number with the fronted COD
Les pommes que j'ai mangées. (COD 'que'=pommes, fem. pl. → mangées)
NEVER agrees, even though 'en' replaces a direct object
Des pommes, j'en ai mangé. (no agreement despite fronted 'en')
No direct object at all (intransitive or indirect verb)
Elle a parlé. / Il a téléphoné à Marie.
