footnotes_tr: Almost exclusively found in subordinate clauses introduced by quand, lorsque, dès que, aussitôt que, à peine... que, followed by a main clause in the passé simple.

tables.caption_tr: Imparfait du Subjonctif — Full Conjugation
footnotes_tr: Formed from the passé simple 2nd person singular stem (tu parlas → parlass-) plus the endings -sse, -sses, ^t (circumflex on the vowel), -ssions, -ssiez, -ssent.

In practice, only the 3rd person singular (qu'il vînt, qu'elle fût, qu'il eût) still appears in contemporary formal/literary writing; the other five persons read as deliberately archaic even to native literary readers.

tables.caption_tr: Plus-que-parfait du Subjonctif — Formation (auxiliary in imparfait du subjonctif + past participle)
footnotes_tr: The 3rd person singular of this tense (il eût aimé, elle eût voulu) doubles as the literary '2nd form' of the conditionnel passé, meaning 'he/she would have liked/wanted', with no subjunctive meaning at all.

tables.caption_tr: Literary Sequence of Tenses (concordance des temps) for the Subjunctive
rows: Past (imparfait, passé simple, passé composé) — simultaneous or later action
Literary: Il fallait qu'il vînt. / Modern: Il fallait qu'il vienne.
Past main clause — prior, completed action
Literary: Elle regretta qu'il fût parti. / Modern: Elle regretta qu'il soit parti.
Literary: Il eût aimé venir. / Modern: Il aurait aimé venir.
footnotes_tr: This strict sequence-of-tense rule is taught as a mark of classical literary style; contemporary spoken and even most written French has simplified it to a single subjonctif présent/passé pairing regardless of the main clause's tense.

tables.caption_tr: Other Markers of Literary and Formal Written Style
rows: Verb placed before the subject pronoun after certain adverbs (peut-être, sans doute, aussi = 'therefore', à peine) or in narrative descriptions
Peut-être viendra-t-il. / À peine fut-il arrivé...
'Expletive ne' with no negative meaning, used after verbs of fear/doubt/prevention, in comparisons, and before avant que, à moins que
Il craint qu'elle ne vienne. / avant qu'il ne parte.
Formal register inserts 'l'' before 'on' after vowel sounds or at the start of a clause, purely for euphony/elegance
Passé simple / passé antérieur replace passé composé / plus-que-parfait as the backbone of narrative prose
Standard in novels, historical accounts, fairy tales
ainsi, or, cependant, néanmoins, dès lors, partant preferred over everyday donc, mais, alors
Or, il advint que le roi mourut.
Multiple embedded subordinate clauses within a single elegant sentence, avoided in everyday speech
Typical of formal essays and 19th-century prose

examples.target: Elle ouvrit la porte et regarda autour d'elle.
examples.translation_tr: She opened the door and looked around her.
examples.note_tr: Passé simple (ouvrit, regarda) — the standard past tense of written narrative; a novel would never use 'a ouvert' here.

examples.target: Dès qu'il eut terminé son discours, l'assemblée applaudit.
examples.translation_tr: As soon as he had finished his speech, the assembly applauded.
examples.note_tr: Passé antérieur (eut terminé) marks an action completed a split second before the passé simple action (applaudit).

examples.target: Il fallait qu'elle partît avant la tombée de la nuit.
examples.translation_tr: It was necessary for her to leave before nightfall.
examples.note_tr: Imparfait du subjonctif (partît) triggered because the main verb 'fallait' is in a past tense — a modern spoken sentence would simply say 'qu'elle parte'.

examples.target: Bien qu'il eût vécu de nombreuses années à l'étranger, il n'oublia jamais sa langue maternelle.
examples.translation_tr: Although he had lived abroad for many years, he never forgot his mother tongue.
examples.note_tr: Plus-que-parfait du subjonctif (eût vécu) expresses an anterior subjunctive action; spoken French would use 'ait vécu'.

examples.target: À peine fut-il arrivé que la tempête éclata.
examples.translation_tr: He had barely arrived when the storm broke out.
examples.note_tr: Passé antérieur + stylistic subject-verb inversion (fut-il), typical after 'à peine' in elevated narration.

examples.target: Peut-être eût-il préféré rester chez lui.
examples.translation_tr: Perhaps he would have preferred to stay home.
examples.note_tr: Plus-que-parfait du subjonctif used as a literary substitute for the second form of the conditionnel passé (= 'il aurait préféré'), with inversion after 'peut-être'.

examples.target: Ce fut alors qu'elle comprit la vérité.
examples.translation_tr: It was then that she understood the truth.
examples.note_tr: Cleft sentence built entirely with passé simple ('fut', 'comprit'), the natural tense of literary storytelling.

examples.target: Quand vint l'automne, les feuilles tombèrent en silence.
examples.translation_tr: When autumn came, the leaves fell silently.
examples.note_tr: Passé simple with inversion (vint l'automne) — a hallmark of descriptive literary prose.

nested-subclauses.title_tr: Nested Subordinate Clauses and Long-Distance Dependencies
nested-subclauses.intro_tr: In formal and literary French, subordinate clauses can be embedded inside other subordinate clauses, creating recursive chains where a relative pronoun, complementizer, or interrogative word is separated from the verb it depends on by several intervening clauses. Standard written French does not allow a "resumptive" pronoun to bridge this distance (unlike some spoken varieties): the linking word appears once at the edge of the whole structure, and the "gap" it fills can lie many clauses down — this is called a long-distance (filler-gap) dependency. Because "que" alone serves as relative pronoun, completive complementizer, comparative marker, and more, chains of "que...que...que" are extremely common in complex written sentences. Tense inside each embedded clause is governed by the sequence-of-tenses rules (concordance des temps) relative to its own immediate matrix clause, and a subjunctive trigger only affects the clause it directly introduces, not clauses nested further inside it. Reading and producing such sentences requires tracking, level by level, which verb governs which clause and where each filler's gap is actually located.

tables.caption_tr: Types of Subordinate Clauses That Can Be Embedded
rows: le livre que tu m'as prêté
Can itself contain another relative or completive clause
Complement of a verb of saying/thinking/feeling
je pense que tu as raison
The single most common source of embedding in French
Complement of a verb of asking/wondering
je me demande si elle sait ce qui s'est passé
Can itself contain a relative clause (ce qui s'est passé)
quand, parce que, bien que, pour que...
quand il est parti, elle a compris que...
Often precedes the matrix clause it modifies
Complement with an implicit shared subject
Avoids one level of finite embedding and a possible subjunctive

tables.caption_tr: Anatomy of a Deeply Embedded Sentence (Level-by-Level Breakdown)
rows: Governs the whole sentence; takes a 'que' complement
Complement of 'crois'; itself takes a 'que' complement
Complement of 'a dit'; itself takes a 'que' complement
que le projet que nous avions proposé
Complement of 'pensait'; contains a relative clause modifying 'le projet'
Main verb of level 4; 'le projet' is the subject whose gap the relative 'que' at level 4 refers to

tables.caption_tr: Long-Distance Relative Dependencies (Filler Pronoun ... Gap Across Clauses)
rows: object of 'avais rencontré', one clause down
C'est l'homme que je pensais que tu avais rencontré hier.
subject of 'était arrivé', one clause down
Voici la personne qui, elle a dit, était arrivée en retard.
complement of 'j'aurais besoin', one clause down
C'est l'outil dont on m'a expliqué que j'aurais besoin.
C'est le livre que je crois que Paul pense que tu devrais lire.

tables.caption_tr: Sequence of Tenses (Concordance des Temps) Inside Nested Clauses
column_headers: Tense of the immediately governing clause
rows: Je pense qu'il travaille / qu'il a fini / qu'il finira.
Je pensais qu'il travaillait / qu'il avait fini / qu'il finirait.
Each level applies its own rule to its own clause
In a chain 'je crois que X a dit que Y pensait que Z...', each 'que'-clause is timed relative to the clause directly above it, not to the outermost matrix verb

tables.caption_tr: Subjunctive Propagation: Where Does It Stop?
rows: the clause introduced by 'que' right after it
not automatically affected unless it has its own trigger
Il faut que tu saches que le train part à huit heures.
'saches' is subjunctive (triggered); 'part' stays indicative because it has no trigger of its own
a further nested clause can be indicative
Je doute qu'il ait dit que c'était vrai.
'ait dit' is subjunctive; 'c'était' is indicative, governed only by 'a dit'
clauses nested inside it follow normal rules
Bien qu'il sache que tu as raison, il refuse d'admettre son erreur.

tables.caption_tr: Common Errors in Long-Distance Dependencies
rows: *C'est l'homme que je pensais que je l'avais rencontré hier.
C'est l'homme que je pensais que j'avais rencontré hier.
Standard written French leaves a silent gap; it does not repeat the pronoun 'l'' inside the embedded clause
Dropping the required 'que' before an embedded clause
Unlike English, French 'que' can never be omitted before a completive clause
Wrong relative pronoun in a stacked relative
Le livre dont je t'ai parlé...
'parler de' requires 'dont', not 'que', even when another relative clause follows on the same antecedent
Mismatched sequence of tenses across levels
*Il a dit qu'il pense que c'est vrai. (mixing past matrix with unadjusted present)
Il a dit qu'il pensait que c'était vrai.
Each embedded clause must shift tense to match the clause immediately governing it, not stay in the present by default
Subjunctive over-propagated to an unrelated deeper clause
*Il faut que tu saches que le train parte à huit heures.
Il faut que tu saches que le train part à huit heures.
Only the clause directly introduced by the trigger takes the subjunctive; deeper clauses with no trigger of their own stay indicative

examples.target: Je crois que Marie a dit qu'elle pensait que le projet que nous avions proposé serait accepté.
examples.translation_tr: I believe that Marie said that she thought that the project we had proposed would be accepted. — four levels of completive embedding (crois > a dit > pensait > serait accepté) plus a relative clause nested inside the deepest 'que'-clause.

examples.target: Le livre dont je t'ai parlé, que tu cherches depuis des mois, vient enfin d'être publié.
examples.translation_tr: The book I told you about, which you've been looking for for months, has finally just been published. — two relative clauses stacked onto the same antecedent 'le livre', using two different relative pronouns (dont / que).

examples.target: Elle se demande si le collègue qui lui avait promis de l'aider viendra.
examples.translation_tr: She wonders whether the colleague who had promised to help her will come. — an indirect question ('si...') containing its own relative clause ('qui...').

examples.target: C'est l'homme que je pensais que tu avais rencontré hier.
examples.translation_tr: That's the man I thought you had met yesterday. — the fronted relative pronoun 'que' fills a gap inside the second 'que'-clause, skipping over 'je pensais'.

examples.target: Il paraît que le témoin que la police recherchait depuis des semaines a enfin été retrouvé.
examples.translation_tr: It seems that the witness the police had been searching for for weeks has finally been found. — an impersonal completive clause contains its own relative clause before reaching its main verb.

examples.target: Que tu réussisses ne signifie pas que tout le monde pensera que tu as eu de la chance.
examples.translation_tr: The fact that you succeed doesn't mean that everyone will think that you were lucky. — a subjunctive-triggering nominal clause as subject, followed by two further nested completive clauses in the indicative.

examples.target: Voici la lettre que j'espère que vous recevrez avant qu'il ne soit trop tard.
examples.translation_tr: Here is the letter that I hope you will receive before it is too late. — a relative clause whose gap sits inside a completive clause, itself followed by a temporal clause using the expletive 'ne'.

examples.target: C'est le genre d'erreur dont on se demande comment quelqu'un d'aussi expérimenté a pu s'en rendre coupable.
examples.translation_tr: It's the kind of mistake one wonders how someone so experienced could have been guilty of. — 'dont' is linked to a gap buried inside an indirect question ('comment...'), showing a long-distance dependency across two clause boundaries.

stylistic-inversion.title_tr: Stylistic Inversion and Heavy Element Shifting
stylistic-inversion.intro_tr: Stylistic inversion (l'inversion stylistique) is a defining feature of formal and literary French, where the subject is placed after the verb instead of before it. It comes in several forms: simple inversion (verb + subject pronoun) used when the subject is already a pronoun, and complex inversion (subject noun + verb + resumptive pronoun) used when the subject is a full noun phrase. A set of sentence-initial adverbs — peut-être, sans doute, aussi (in its causal sense), ainsi, à peine, du moins, encore — trigger or favor this inversion in careful written style, though everyday spoken French usually avoids it by adding 'que' or keeping normal word order. A closely related phenomenon is heavy element shifting, whereby long or syntactically complex subjects are postposed to the end of the clause (especially after relative pronouns and with verbs of appearance, arrival, or existence) so that the sentence moves naturally from light to heavy elements. Together these patterns are essential for reading and writing sophisticated, literary-register French, and they appear constantly in journalism, essays, and narrative prose.

tables.caption_tr: Sentence-Initial Adverbs Triggering Stylistic Inversion
rows: Peut-être viendra-t-il demain. / Peut-être qu'il viendra demain.
Both correct; inversion sounds more formal/literary
Common in formal writing and journalism
Il pleuvait fort; aussi resta-t-il chez lui.
Only the causal 'aussi' triggers inversion; additive 'aussi' (=also) does not
À peine était-il arrivé qu'il repartit.
Usually paired with a following 'que' clause
Frozen formal idiom meaning 'that still needs to be proven'
Tout au plus pourrait-on regretter son silence.

tables.caption_tr: Simple vs. Complex Inversion — Structural Comparison
rows: Subject is already a pronoun (je, tu, il, elle, on, nous, vous, ils, elles)
Subject noun (stays in place) + Verb + resumptive pronoun
Subject is a noun or proper noun; the noun stays before the verb, and a pronoun echoing it follows the verb
Ainsi parla Zarathoustra. / Alors vint le printemps.
Literary/narrative style, typically with intransitive verbs of movement, appearance, or existence; closely tied to heavy-subject postposition
Verb + hyphenated subject pronoun, with liaison -t-
Question formation — same mechanics as stylistic inversion but a different grammatical function

tables.caption_tr: Heavy Element Shifting: Postposing Long or Complex Subjects
rows: Relative clauses with a long/complex subject
Relative pronoun + Verb + heavy subject NP
Voici le livre dont a parlé le critique le plus influent de sa génération.
The heavy subject NP is postposed after the verb because it is longer/more complex than staying preverbal would allow
Verbs of appearance, existence, or movement (arriver, survenir, apparaître, rester, venir, surgir)
Alors surgit une immense clameur venue de la foule.
Very common in literary and journalistic narration
After relative/interrogative words (où, quand, comment, que)
La ville où s'est déroulée la conférence internationale sur le climat.
Keeps the light connector near the start of the clause and the heavy subject at the end
Subject pronoun stays before the verb — no postposition
La ville où il est né.
Postposition mainly applies to full noun phrases, not simple pronouns
Il est plus compétent que ne l'était son prédécesseur.

tables.caption_tr: Inversion in Reporting Clauses (Incises)
rows: Complex inversion's resumptive pronoun is not used here — the noun simply follows the verb
Only the auxiliary inverts with the subject
Le projet, affirme-t-il, sera achevé à temps.
Common way to attribute a claim without starting a new sentence

tables.caption_tr: Register Comparison: Everyday Speech vs. Formal/Literary French
rows: Il a peut-être raison. / Peut-être qu'il a raison.
He was tired, so he stayed home
Il était fatigué, alors il est resté à la maison.
Il était fatigué; aussi resta-t-il à la maison.
Il faut quand même le prouver.
Il venait tout juste d'arriver quand...
La réunion s'est terminée comme ça.

tables.caption_tr: Common Mistakes and Key Exceptions
rows: Inversion always requires hyphens linking the verb and the subject pronoun
Insert '-t-' between a vowel-final verb form and il/elle/on
Use simple inversion only — do not add a resumptive pronoun when the subject is already a pronoun
Il est riche, aussi il est généreux.
Il est riche et il est aussi généreux. (additive, no inversion) / Il est riche; aussi est-il généreux. (causal, needs inversion)
Causal 'aussi' (= therefore) requires inversion; additive 'aussi' (= also) does not
Voici le livre dont a parlé il.
Voici le livre dont il a parlé.
Heavy-element postposition applies to full noun phrases, not pronoun subjects
Once 'que' is used, normal (non-inverted) word order follows; choose one strategy, not both

examples.target: Peut-être est-il déjà parti.
examples.translation_tr: Perhaps he has already left.
examples.note_tr: Simple inversion with 'peut-être'; 'est' + 't' + 'il' for euphony.

examples.target: Ainsi s'achève notre histoire.
examples.translation_tr: Thus our story ends.
examples.note_tr: Literary/narrative inversion after 'ainsi' (thus).

examples.target: À peine avait-elle fermé la porte que le téléphone sonna.
examples.translation_tr: She had scarcely closed the door when the phone rang.
examples.note_tr: 'À peine... que' pattern with obligatory inversion in the main clause.

examples.target: Voici la lettre qu'a écrite ma grand-mère avant sa mort.
examples.translation_tr: Here is the letter that my grandmother wrote before her death.
examples.note_tr: Heavy subject 'ma grand-mère' postposed after the verb in a relative clause.

examples.target: « Je ne reviendrai jamais », murmura-t-il.
examples.translation_tr: "I will never come back," he murmured.
examples.note_tr: Inversion in a reporting clause (incise) after direct speech.

examples.target: Il était plus doué que ne le pensaient ses professeurs.
examples.translation_tr: He was more talented than his teachers thought.
examples.note_tr: Inversion after comparative 'que' with 'ne explétif' and a heavy subject.

examples.target: Sans doute a-t-elle ses raisons.
examples.translation_tr: She probably has her reasons.
examples.note_tr: Formal alternative to 'Elle a sans doute ses raisons' (no inversion needed in the neutral order).

examples.target: Alors apparut, au loin, une lumière étrange.
examples.translation_tr: Then, in the distance, a strange light appeared.
examples.note_tr: Pure stylistic inversion with an intransitive verb of appearance and a heavy postposed subject.

archaic-fixed-forms.title_tr: Fossilized Archaic Structures (fût-il, d'aucuns, n'eût été)
archaic-fixed-forms.intro_tr: French has preserved a handful of fossilized literary constructions inherited from Classical and Old French syntax that survive today only as fixed idioms or in highly formal registers (journalism, legal writing, literature, proverbs). These include inverted subjonctif-imparfait concessive forms like "fût-il" ("even if it/he were") and "dût-il" ("even if he had to"), the archaic indefinite pronoun "aucuns" in "d'aucuns" ("some people"), and the counterfactual "n'eût été" ("had it not been for"). Because these forms follow obsolete grammar rules — stylistic inversion, the subjonctif plus-que-parfait used as a substitute for the conditionnel passé, and pronouns no longer used elsewhere — they cannot be generated productively from ordinary rules; each one must simply be memorized as a set phrase. You will almost never need to produce these forms yourself, but recognizing them is essential for reading elevated French: newspaper editorials, court judgments, official speeches, and 19th-century literature are full of them.

tables.caption_tr: Inverted Subjunctive Concessive Forms (fût-il, dût-il, n'eût été...)
rows: subjonctif imparfait of être + inverted subject pronoun
même s'il était / même si c'était
concessive clause at the start of a sentence, no 'si'
subjonctif imparfait of être, plural, inverted
même s'il devait / même s'ils devaient
expresses 'at the risk of', 'whatever it costs him'
subjonctif imparfait of devoir, 1st person, inverted
negative subjonctif plus-que-parfait of avoir + past participle
s'il n'y avait pas eu... / sans...
counterfactual, replaces 'si cela n'avait pas été'
present counterfactual (less remote than n'eût été)
minimizes the following element: 'ne serait-ce qu'un instant'
footnotes_tr: All of these forms place the verb before the subject pronoun and drop 'si'; this stylistic inversion alone signals the concessive or counterfactual meaning.
In everyday speech these are replaced by 'même si + indicative' or 'sans + noun'.

tables.caption_tr: Reference: Subjonctif Imparfait / Plus-que-parfait of être, avoir, devoir (the forms behind the inversions above)
column_headers: avoir (subj. plus-que-parfait, base for n'eût été)
footnotes_tr: Only the 3rd person singular and plural forms (fût, fussent, eût, eussent, dût, dussent) are commonly seen in the fixed inverted expressions; the other persons exist mainly for grammatical completeness or highly literary first-person concessions like 'dussé-je'.

tables.caption_tr: Archaic Pronouns and Quantifiers Surviving in Fixed Expressions
rows: always used as a subject pronoun, never with 'de' before a noun; found in journalistic/literary register
survives in the proverb 'nul n'est censé ignorer la loi' (ignorance of the law is no excuse)
fixed in the expression 'maintes fois' (many a time)
now archaic to the point of sounding humorous or ironic in modern speech
footnotes_tr: Unlike modern indefinite pronouns (quelqu'un, certains, chacun), these archaic forms are frozen: they cannot be freely combined with other determiners or used in new constructions.

tables.caption_tr: Fixed Archaic Idiomatic Expressions in Formal/Literary Registers
rows: for better or worse, somehow or other
at all costs, whatever it takes
still fairly common in formal speech
far from it, by no means
in so doing, by doing this
incidentally, be it said in passing
the fact remains that, be that as it may
footnotes_tr: These expressions are entirely invariable: none of their component words can be changed, reordered, or replaced without breaking the idiom.
Most remain productive in formal written French today, unlike the grammatically 'dead' inversions in Table 1, which are essentially quotation-only relics outside of set phrases.

examples.target: Fût-il le meilleur candidat, il devra tout de même convaincre le jury.
examples.translation_tr: Even if he were the best candidate, he would still have to convince the jury.
examples.note_tr: 'Fût-il' = subjonctif imparfait of être + inverted subject, used as a literary concessive meaning 'even if he were'.

examples.target: D'aucuns pensent que cette réforme est inutile, mais je ne partage pas cet avis.
examples.translation_tr: Some people think this reform is useless, but I don't share that opinion.
examples.note_tr: 'D'aucuns' is an archaic indefinite pronoun meaning 'some (people)'; it is always followed directly by a verb, never by 'de'.

examples.target: N'eût été son intervention rapide, la situation aurait dégénéré.
examples.translation_tr: Had it not been for his quick intervention, the situation would have escalated.
examples.note_tr: 'N'eût été' = negative subjonctif plus-que-parfait of avoir, functioning as a counterfactual 'had it not been for'.

examples.target: Dût-il en payer le prix, il ira jusqu'au bout de son projet.
examples.translation_tr: Even if he has to pay the price for it, he will see his project through to the end.
examples.note_tr: 'Dût-il' = subjonctif imparfait of devoir, inverted, meaning 'even if he had to / at the risk of'.

examples.target: Coûte que coûte, nous terminerons ce rapport avant vendredi.
examples.translation_tr: Whatever it takes, we will finish this report before Friday.
examples.note_tr: Fixed, invariable expression meaning 'no matter the cost / at all costs'.

examples.target: Toujours est-il qu'il a fini par démissionner de son poste.
examples.translation_tr: The fact remains that he eventually resigned from his position.
examples.note_tr: Fixed inverted formula introducing a fact that stands regardless of what precedes it.

examples.target: Peu s'en faut qu'il ait tout perdu dans cette affaire.
examples.translation_tr: He very nearly lost everything in this matter.
examples.note_tr: 'Peu s'en faut que' + subjunctive means 'it lacks little that...' i.e. 'very nearly'.

examples.target: Ainsi soit-il, conclut le prêtre à la fin de la prière.
examples.translation_tr: So be it, the priest concluded at the end of the prayer.
examples.note_tr: Fossilized subjunctive formula, the French equivalent of liturgical 'amen'.

francophone-varieties.title_tr: Francophone Varieties: Québec, Belgian, and Swiss French
francophone-varieties.intro_tr: Standard (Metropolitan/Parisian) French is only one variety among several official forms of French used across the Francophonie. Québec, Belgium, and Switzerland each developed distinct vocabulary, numeral systems, syntactic quirks, and pronunciation features shaped by history and contact with other languages (English in Québec; Dutch/Flemish in Belgium; German and Italian in Switzerland). At the C2 level, recognizing these regionalisms matters for reading authentic texts, understanding media, and avoiding the false assumption that "French" means only the Parisian standard. This page focuses on the differences most likely to appear in writing and formal recognition tasks: the number system (70–99), everyday vocabulary, meal-name shifts, grammar/syntax patterns, and key pronunciation tendencies.

tables.caption_tr: Numbers 70–99: Regional Systems Compared
rows: France builds 70 as '60+10'; Belgium/Switzerland use the simpler Latin-derived 'septante'.
Pattern continues regularly with 'et un' for 1.
Belgium always uses 'quatre-vingts' like France; only some Swiss cantons use 'huitante'.
Belgium and Switzerland avoid the French '80+10' construction entirely.
The nonante-based system is fully regular, unlike the standard French vigesimal-based forms.

tables.caption_tr: Everyday Vocabulary: France vs Québec vs Belgium vs Switzerland
rows: faire du shopping / faire les courses
faire du shopping / courir les magasins

tables.caption_tr: Meal Names: The Québec Shift
footnotes_tr: This is a systematic one-step shift: what France calls 'déjeuner' (lunch), Québec calls 'dîner', and so on. This reflects older French usage preserved in Québec after colonial-era divergence from Metropolitan norms.

tables.caption_tr: Grammar and Syntax Features by Region
rows: Adds emphatic 'tu' after the verb in informal spoken questions; not written in formal registers.
Archaic/regional form of 'aller' preserved from older French, used informally.
Je suis en amour avec lui.
Calque of English 'in love with', vs Standard French 'amoureux de lui'.
Untranslatable filler softening a command/request, from Dutch/Flemish influence.
Used when handing something over, unlike France where it only means 'please'.
'Natel' (mobile phone), 'witz' (joke) are loanwords absent from Standard French.
Used in French-speaking cantons like Vaud and Valais, not in Geneva or Jura.

rows: Pronounced closer to [tsy], [dzy]; a hallmark of Québécois accent.
Vowels are lengthened and glide, giving a distinctive 'sung' quality.
Clear distinction between 'brin' and 'brun' nasal vowels
This distinction has merged in most of France but is retained in Belgium.
Devoicing of final consonants less common
Final consonants tend to stay clearly voiced, differing subtly from Parisian French.
Less of the typical French stress pattern; syllables are more evenly timed.
Vowel oppositions that are merging in France remain distinct in Swiss French.

examples.target: Tu viens-tu avec nous à soir?
examples.translation_tr: Are you coming with us tonight? (Québec, colloquial 'tu' used as a spoken question marker, plus 'à soir' = 'ce soir')
examples.note_tr: Non-standard 'tu' interrogative particle is typical of informal Québécois speech and would sound odd or ungrammatical in France.

examples.target: Il fait septante balles, ce manteau.
examples.translation_tr: This coat costs seventy bucks. (Belgium/Switzerland: 'septante' = 70, instead of France's 'soixante-dix')
examples.note_tr: 'Balles' is informal for 'francs/euros', similar to English 'bucks'.

examples.target: As-tu déjà magasiné pour ton chum?
examples.translation_tr: Have you already shopped for your boyfriend? (Québec: 'magasiner' = to shop, 'chum' = boyfriend)
examples.note_tr: 'Magasiner' and 'chum' are everyday Québécois words absent from Metropolitan French usage.

examples.target: Une fois, tu me passes le sel?
examples.translation_tr: Could you pass me the salt? (Belgium: filler 'une fois' softens a request, roughly like English 'just')
examples.note_tr: This filler use of 'une fois' has no literal translation and is a well-known Belgian French marker.

examples.target: Mon natel est déchargé, je ne peux pas t'appeler.
examples.translation_tr: My cellphone is dead, I can't call you. (Switzerland: 'natel' = mobile phone, from a Swiss brand name)
examples.note_tr: France uses 'portable', Belgium often uses 'GSM', Québec uses 'cellulaire'.

examples.target: On va souper vers dix-huit heures.
examples.translation_tr: We're going to have dinner around 6 p.m. (Québec: 'souper' = evening meal, matching older/regional French usage)
examples.note_tr: In Québec the meal names shift one step earlier than in France: déjeuner=breakfast, dîner=lunch, souper=dinner.

examples.target: Il neige à plein temps depuis ce matin.
examples.translation_tr: It's been snowing non-stop since this morning. (Québec idiom 'à plein temps' used adverbially for 'constantly')
examples.note_tr: This figurative extension of a work-related expression is a Québécois usage, not found in Standard French.

examples.target: S'il vous plaît, voici votre monnaie.
examples.translation_tr: Here you go, here's your change. (Belgium: 's'il vous plaît' can mean 'here you go' when handing something over)
examples.note_tr: In France, 's'il vous plaît' only means 'please'; this handing-over usage is a distinctly Belgian (and Swiss) calque of Dutch/German equivalents.

idiomatic-structures.intro_tr: French is exceptionally rich in fixed idiomatic expressions (idiotismes) and proverbs (proverbes) whose meaning cannot be derived from the literal sum of their words, and whose internal grammar often freezes older or unusual syntactic patterns no longer productive in everyday speech. Mastering them at a C2 level means recognizing recurring structural templates — elliptical parallelism (tel...tel), headless relative clauses (qui...), correlative comparatives (plus...plus), and cleft constructions with a gerund (c'est en...que) — as well as memorizing thematic vocabulary fields (body parts, animals, colors, weather) that idioms draw on. Because these expressions are lexically and syntactically fossilized, word order, prepositions, and even archaic subjunctive forms inside them cannot be altered or translated word-for-word. This page organizes the most useful idioms and proverbs by theme and isolates the grammatical patterns that make proverbial French sound distinctively 'proverbial' rather than merely figurative.

tables.caption_tr: Grammatical patterns unique to idiomatic and proverbial syntax
rows: Two parallel noun phrases with no linking verb, implying resemblance
Tel père, tel fils. (Like father, like son.)
'Qui' used without any antecedent, meaning 'whoever/the one who' — an archaic, formulaic use
Qui vivra verra. / Qui dort dîne.
A fragment stands alone as a fixed saying, the original verb having disappeared over time
À bon entendeur, salut. (A word to the wise is enough.)
Emphasizes the means/manner of an action inside a cleft sentence built around a gerund
C'est en forgeant qu'on devient forgeron. (Practice makes perfect.)
Two parallel comparative clauses expressing a proportional relationship
Plus on est de fous, plus on rit.
Double negative structure frozen inside a set expression, often without a verb
Ni vu, ni connu. (No one saw or knew — got away with it.)
Archaic present subjunctive used alone to express a wish or resignation
Advienne que pourra. / Vive la République !
Verb-subject inversion for an elevated, aphoristic tone typical of proverbs
Ainsi va le monde. (Such is the way of the world.)

examples.target: Ne vends pas la peau de l'ours avant de l'avoir tué : attends les résultats officiels.
examples.translation_tr: Don't count your chickens before they hatch: wait for the official results.
examples.note_tr: Literally 'don't sell the bear's skin before killing it' — a proverb warning against premature celebration.

examples.target: Il pleut à torrents depuis ce matin, mais après la pluie, le beau temps.
examples.translation_tr: It's been pouring since this morning, but every cloud has a silver lining.
examples.note_tr: The proverb functions as a standalone clause with no verb — a fixed elliptical saying.

examples.target: Elle a posé un lapin à son rendez-vous hier soir.
examples.translation_tr: She stood up her date last night.
examples.note_tr: 'Poser un lapin' has nothing to do with rabbits; it is a fully fossilized idiom.

examples.target: C'est en forgeant qu'on devient forgeron, alors continue à t'entraîner.
examples.translation_tr: Practice makes perfect, so keep training.
examples.note_tr: A cleft sentence (c'est... que) built around a gérondif, typical of proverbial syntax.

examples.target: Il a ri jaune quand on lui a annoncé la nouvelle.
examples.translation_tr: He gave a forced, nervous laugh when told the news.
examples.note_tr: Color idiom: 'rire jaune' = to laugh insincerely, masking discomfort.

examples.target: Petit à petit, l'oiseau fait son nid : sois patient avec ton projet.
examples.translation_tr: Slow and steady wins the race: be patient with your project.
examples.note_tr: Progressive repetition ('petit à petit') plus a metaphorical main clause is a classic proverb template.

examples.target: Mon collègue a un chat dans la gorge aujourd'hui, il ne peut presque plus parler.
examples.translation_tr: My colleague has a frog in his throat today; he can barely speak.
examples.note_tr: Animal-based idiom for hoarseness; note French uses 'chat' where English uses 'frog'.

examples.target: Qui vivra verra ce que l'avenir nous réserve.
examples.translation_tr: Time will tell what the future holds for us.
examples.note_tr: 'Qui' here is a headless relative pronoun meaning 'whoever' — an archaic, proverbial usage.
